articles.title_orig: Live updates: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez speaks at UN months after US captured her predecessor
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez speaks at UN months after US captured her predecessor
articles.content_orig:
• All eyes on Venezuela: The country’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez addressed the UN General Assembly more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro. She said Venezuela will hold elections and transition to a full democracy — but didn’t specify when — and thanked US President Donald Trump for his “readiness” toward diplomacy.
• Iran president speaks: Earlier, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will not bend to Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” Separately, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said US-Iran mediated talks did not yield any major breakthrough.
• Zelensky’s warning: In his remarks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the Russian leader spreads war and instability. As he spoke, Zelensky’s party headquarters were struck by Russia, according to Kyiv officials.
Spain PM calls for reforming the UN Security Council
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for strengthening the function of the United Nations (UN), adding that a necessary step toward this goal is reforming the Security Council and eliminating the veto power held by its five permanent members.
In his address to the UN General Assembly this evening, Sánchez argued that these measures would help revitalize multilateralism.
“We need to reform the Security Council to ensure fair representation for all regions of the world and to end the veto power of permanent members, because, as the UN Charter indicates, no country — no matter how powerful — should act as both judge and party to a dispute,” he said.
Earlier, during his own address, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino also proposed reforming the Security Council to grant permanent membership to countries from Latin America and the Caribbean.
The Security Council currently consists of 15 members: 10 non-permanent and five permanent members with veto power (the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Russia, and China).
Delcy Rodríguez thanks Trump for "willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations"
Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez thanked President Donald Trump this evening for what she called “his willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation” with her country.
During her debut address to the United Nations General Assembly, Rodríguez said Venezuela seeks to “be reborn” following two blows suffered this year: first, the “strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States”; and second, the double earthquakes of June 24.
The earthquakes were devastating toVenezuela, causing the deaths of more than 6,500 people and extensive material damage.
Venezuela to hold elections, transition to democracy, acting president tells UNGA
Venezuela will hold elections and transition to a full democracy, acting President Delcy Rodríguez said Wednesday at the UN General Assembly.
Rodríguez didn’t specify when a vote will be held, only saying that the Venezuelan people will “determine when the correct time for these elections is.”
Rodríguez, who became acting president after the United States toppled strongman leader Nicolás Maduro, said the democratic transition is underway and promised that the process would be transparent, inclusive and verifiable.
“We have begun a political dialogue with sectors of the opposition, which will lead to a process where everyone will compete on an equal footing,” she said.
Rodriguez delivered her speech a day after Venezuela’s exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado attempted to return to the country but was denied entry three times, according to her advisers.
A look at the current state of US-Venezuela relations
On January 3, US forces undertook a high-stakes operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from a compound in Caracas and transport him to the US to face criminal charges.
Maduro’s vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, assumed the position of acting president. Since then, Rodríguez, a stalwart of both the Hugo Chávez and Maduro governments, has worked to win US President Donald Trump’s support while keeping Chavismo alive.
Rodríguez, who is speaking today at the UN General Assembly, has overseen tactical concessions to Washington, including favorable positions in strategic sectors like oil, and permitting increased US oversight and presence in the country. Meanwhile, much has stayed the same inside Venezuela under her rule, and little progress has been made toward holding democratic elections.
In August, the Venezuelan government met with opposition figures to begin US-backed talks aimed toward a democratic transition. On September 2, Trump said Venezuela is “not going to be ready” for democratic elections but looks forward to holding them “soon.”
In June, Rodríguez confronted the biggest crisis of her tenure so far when catastrophic earthquakes killed thousands and injured and displaced tens of thousands more. The US State Department said it would provide $150 million in aid to Venezuela in the aftermath of the tragedy.
The evolving relationship was most recently highlighted by a deal between the two countries that gave the US majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves, according to Trump.
CNN’s Betsy Klein, Anabella González, Germán Padinger, Michael Rios, Kit Maher and Alfredo Meza contributed reporting.
European Council president meets Iran’s Pezeshkian on UNGA sidelines
European Council President Antonio Costa met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and called on Iran to cease strikes on its neighbors.
Costa said the two leaders had a “frank and substantial discussion,” and urged Iran to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, which has been a major point of contention in the Iran war.
“I stressed that dialogue is the only way to resolve conflicts and to ensure lasting peace across the region,” Costa posted to X.
Costa also urged Iran to resume cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Iran has said it will not comply with demands from the agency to inspect its bombed nuclear sites, citing the absence of established regulations for inspecting facilities damaged by military strikes.
In June, Israel and the United States carried out significant military strikes targeting Iran’s nuclear program, damaging key sites including Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan.
How Venezuela's Delcy Rodríguez faced her worst crisis yet after devastating earthquakes
The devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela in late June would have tested any government. But they hit a country still navigating the aftermath of strongman Nicolás Maduro’s capture nearly 10 months ago, turning a natural disaster into a political test for acting President Delcy Rodríguez and exposing anger over the state’s response.
The two catastrophic earthquakes that struck in quick succession on June 24 have left more than 6,500 dead, according to figures released in late August by the President of the National Assembly of Venezuela, Jorge Rodríguez.
Both inside and outside the country, many citizens claimed authorities responded too slowly and failed to adequately address the tragedy, a criticism Rodríguez firmly rejects.
Analysts interviewed by CNN say the earthquakes have become a defining test for the interim government, exposing its political vulnerability and the limits of the state’s power to respond to the disaster. They argue that its outcome remains highly uncertain and that the actions of the United States will be decisive, given the supervisory role Washington currently plays in Venezuela.
The June 24 earthquakes rank among the deadliest natural disasters in Venezuela’s history.

articles.title_orig: Meta VR Glasses Officially Announced, Shipping Spring 2027 For $1300
articles.title_zh: Meta VR Glasses Officially Announced, Shipping Spring 2027 For $1300
articles.content_orig:
Meta VR Glasses were just officially announced. Priced at $1300, they have 2.4K micro-OLED displays, weigh 100 grams, and are powered by a tethered puck with Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset.
The puck runs the same operating system as Quest 3, and supports all the same content, rendered at notably higher resolution thanks to a combination of the more powerful chipset (essentially an XR2 Gen 3 by a different name) and eye-tracked foveated rendering. It features 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, and there's a microSD slot in the puck to expand it.
The caveat to the content compatibility is that Meta VR Glasses do not come with controllers by default, but you can buy Touch Plus controllers separately (available in a new all-black color), or pair the controllers from your existing Quest 3 or Quest 3S, and there'll be a bundle with controllers "in some retail channels".
The stark difference between Meta VR Glasses and any Quest, however, is the split architecture, and the dramatic reduction in weight and bulk this enables.
Meta VR Glasses have no onboard computing, not even a tracking coprocessor, and thus entirely rely on the puck, which provides both power and data over a thin and flexible fiber optic cable.
The visor has an open-periphery design, so you naturally see the real world to your sides and below you. It's built with a magnesium alloy that minimizes weight while also enabling a fanless, passively cooled design that weighs "around" 100 grams.
Another key difference is the display and field of view. With dual 120Hz 2412×2288 HDR micro-OLED displays, Meta VR Glasses have the highest resolution of any Meta headset to date, and are the company's first non-LCD headset since the original Oculus Quest.
The displays support the Dolby Vision HDR format, Meta says it's the first VR device to be IMAX Enhanced certified.
The form factor brings a major optical compromise, though: the field of view. Meta advertises 70° horizontal × 66° vertical (equating to 87° diagonal) compared to the roughly 110° horizontal × 96° vertical of Quest 3.
The lower field of view will make Meta VR Glasses feel far less immersive than a Quest headset when the optional light blockers are attached for fully immersive experiences. But, somewhat ironically given the name of the product, Meta VR Glasses should shine without the light blockers in passthrough mixed reality, where a natural view of your periphery is arguably preferable to darkness.
Meta plans to market the product as "a private cinema, multiple virtual monitor workspace, and game console in one device that fits in your bag".
Essentially, Meta VR Glasses at its core is the same product proposition as the Xreal Aura Android XR glasses but with a VR-style passthrough display system that offers a larger field of view (87° diagonal vs Xreal's 70°), higher resolution, and full opacity, alongside the inclusion of eye tracking and optional tracked controllers. We do not yet know the price of Xreal Aura.
To expand the library of content available to all Meta VR Glasses buyers, Meta announced a swathe of new hand tracking VR and mixed reality games, including a new hand-tracked Beat Saber mode called Flux. You can read about the gaming announcements here.
For the first time for a Meta standalone device, you can also plug in any USB-C DisplayPort device to the puck and have it shown as a huge virtual screen in Meta VR Glasses, without the need for a capture card.
Meta VR Glasses will also feature the first implementation of Hologram, the company's productization of its Codec Avatars research. Similar to Apple Vision Pro's Personas, it will let you join flatscreen WhatsApp video calls as a photorealistic face-tracked avatar, and appear as a realistic full-scale avatar for other Meta VR Glasses (and eventually Quest 3) owners.
However, at launch in spring, your spatial Hologram will be a "2.5D" stereoscopic video stream, at true scale but only seen as a front-angle view. Even if you change your perspective, the Hologram will stay as a head-on perspective. Meta says it plans to evolve Hologram over time to become a truly 6DoF 3D system, at which point it will become the default platform-level avatar experience for its VR platform, effectively superseding the cartoon Meta Avatars.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
articles.content_orig:
Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, saying Iranians are "the victims of terrorism" by the U.S. and Israel, and have "never ever been an aggressor."
- A commercial vessel was struck in an attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, killing one crew member and necessitating the evacuation of more than 20 more sailors, according to the Omani navy.
- U.S. and Iranian officials met Tuesday while both countries were at the U.N. gathering, President Trump said, shortly after threatening in his address that he may "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
8 suicide attempts by U.S. sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln strike group during its record-long deployment, Navy letter says
There were eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since it began its record-long deployment about 10 months ago, according to a letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that was obtained Wednesday by CBS News.
CNN was first to report on the letter. A Navy official confirmed it was sent Tuesday.
The deployment of the Lincoln and its approximately 5,000 crew members came under scrutiny after family members of the sailors and members of Congress raised questions last month about the conditions aboard the carrier and concerns about the mental health of its service members.
The Lincoln and its strike group were sent to the Middle East after the Iran war broke out. It has since left the region and is returning to its home base of San Diego.
A defense official told CBS News two of the suicide attempts occurred during active fighting with Iran. The letter covers the entire length of the Lincoln strike group's deployment, which began in November of last year.
The strike group includes the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all the embarked aviation squadrons.
The letter was in response to questions from Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York about reported conditions on the ship. In a statement provided to CBS News, Gillibrand said that what President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members."
That the Trump administration "can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable," she added.
U.S. blockade has redirected 115 commercial vessels, military says
The U.S. military blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 115 commercial vessels entering or exiting Iranian ports, according to U.S. Central Command.
The total is an increase of five ships since Monday, when the military last provided an update.
The blockade has become a renewed topic of conflict as Iran and the U.S. renewed negotiations this week at the U.N. General Assembly. Representatives from the United States, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Iranian officials on Tuesday and apparently found some common ground, with President Trump saying the meetings went well.
However, on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei reiterated that no deal will be signed until the U.S. removes the blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
White House responds to Iranian president's speech at U.N.
President Trump is "courageously" fighting against the Iranian regime, the White House said Tuesday in response to a question about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's speech at the U.N. General Assembly.
"The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable."
Through a translator, Pezeshkian said Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."
Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said.
Canada imposes new sanctions on Iran officials, entities
The Canadian government announced new sanctions Wednesday against several senior Iranian officials and state-run entities "for their role in the Iranian regime's brutal repression of its population."
The sanctions target five senior Iranian security and government officials and five state-run entities, the foreign ministry said in a statement, without providing specifics.
"These individuals and entities have contributed to Iran's efforts to suppress dissent and restrict fundamental freedoms of Iran's population, including through digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation," the ministry said.
A protest movement in Iran sparked in late December by grievances over high living costs rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on Jan. 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths from the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Rights groups based abroad put the toll higher and accused security forces of firing at demonstrators.
Massive protests also erupted in Iran in Sep. 2022 following the death in custody of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for allegedly violating strict dress rules for women.
UAE sanctions local branches of Iran's Bank Melli
The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers."
It cited "non-compliance with the regulations, laws and supervisory decisions in force in the UAE, including the requirements and obligations set out under the legislation related to combating money laundering, the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing."
The announcement comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, as well as Washington's more recent economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic.
As part of that stepped-up campaign, the U.S. announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Bank Melli.
Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran.
German foreign minister: "Iran must engage constructively" in negotiations
Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, offered a direct criticism of Iranian negotiations in a meeting with his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Iran must engage constructively in talks for a sustainable solution to end the conflict in the region & unconditionally open the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring free, safe and toll-free navigation for all," he said on social media.
Wadephul's comments came as Iran continues to take a hard line in negotiations, demanding the U.S. remove its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, end the war on all fronts, release frozen or restricted assets and agree to the Oman-Iran negotiated passage through the strait, acco

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Soaring Treasury yields aren't just bad for the government and its $40 trillion debt. They also threaten to raise borrowing costs, hitting everyone from homeowners to credit card users, while providing limited relief to savers and potential benefits to banks.
Government debt costs leaped higher Wednesday, the product of multiple factors including a fresh report showing higher inflation pressures, surging expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, and an auction for 5-year notes showing that Treasury demand was weak. Competition from hyperscaler debt issuance also is seen as an aggravating factor.
Yields responded by jumping more than they have in nearly a year and a half, dating back to April 2025 when President Donald Trump first announced so-called reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. Recent market liquidity efforts pushed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have had no impact so far, with rates surging higher despite intensified buyback efforts on longer-dated debt.
The 10-year note, a benchmark for mortgages and other longer-term borrowing, saw its yield hit, 5.125%, a level not seen since prior to the global financial crisis. Similarly, the 2-year note, which typically responds to Fed rate expectations and signals rates for home equity, auto loans and other debt, climbed more than 13 basis points past 4.9% as traders priced in a strong possibility that the central bank would follow its hike last week with another in October.
One basis point equals 0.01% and yields move opposite prices.
Such moves generally portend higher borrowing rates that hit the U.S. economy where it hurts the most — consumers, who drive nearly 70% of all economic activity and hold nearly $19 trillion in total debt.
While savers will benefit with incrementally higher rates on their bank savings accounts, it's unlikely to offset the pain they'll feel elsewhere, said Dan North, senior economist with Allianz Trade North America.
"The consumer's the most important part of the economy," North said. "They're going from little tiny yields on savings to ever slightly bigger tiny yields on savings. So I don't think that really yet helps the consumer that much. But it sure does crush housing, and it [impacts] on all those personal consumer loans, the credit cards and so forth."
Indeed, the interest rate on plain-vanilla savings accounts is around 0.37% and has been on a modest decline since the Fed enacted three quarter-point cuts late in 2025, according to FDIC data.
Mortgage rates, though, have been on an entirely different trajectory and are likely to continue rising. A typical 30-year mortgage is now at 7.26%, up more than a quarter percentage point in just the past couple weeks and nearly a full point over the past year, according to Mortgage News Daily.
Credit card interest rates have been fairly steady over the past few years, but also are unlikely to stay that way if current trends hold up.
When the Fed hikes, it feeds directly into the prime rate, which is used as a baseline for adjustable-rate credit and most recently was at 7%, after rising a quarter point off last week's Fed move.
Taken together, the factors make it more expensive for consumers to borrow and less likely that they'll seek the loans and credit that fuel a lot of the activity in the $32 trillion U.S. economy.
"You raise the fed funds rate, rates in the short term and effectively all along the curve go up," North said. "If it makes it harder for somebody to buy a car, then there's less demand for cars and there's less demand for auto workers, and the economy slows down. That's sort of basic economics, but that's how it works."
There are some positives from the higher rates.
Aside from whatever benefit savers get, banks can benefit. The industry's model is based on a variety of factors that can benefit in times of higher rates, from what they can charge borrowers to the margin they earn from what they charge to what they pay depositors, as well as the opportunity to get better return on their cash.
However, even bank stocks were mostly lower Wednesday as dramatically higher yields could slow loan demand and broader economic activity, which otherwise has been solid. The Atlanta Fed is tracking GDP growth of 5.1% for the third quarter, another element that could be factoring into higher yields.
Persistently higher yields, though, pose dangers to that growth picture.
"Smaller and medium enterprises are going to be suffering the worst because they have less ability to borrow," North said. "Less availability of credit makes it more difficult."

articles.content_orig:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital on Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of each other, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us," he said.
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faced a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now," he added,
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy.
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved," Taleblu said.

"Of course, the Trump administration is looking for a political win here," he concluded.

articles.title_orig: Judge set to rule on Trump administration’s rationale for White House media ban
articles.title_zh: Judge set to rule on Trump administration’s rationale for White House media ban
articles.content_orig:
The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House were in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be blocked immediately.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly did not immediately rule on the request after hearing arguments from an attorney for CNN, Politico and MS NOW and a lawyer for the Justice Department.
During the roughly 45-minute hearing, Kelly, a Trump appointee, appeared particularly focused on the “due process” — or lack thereof — that the journalists whose hard passes were revoked received.
He said due process requirements laid out by the judges in earlier cases involving press access, including the appeals court, were not followed in this case. “The government says those cases were wrongly decided,” Kelly said, but he has a “duty” to apply them in this case.
In a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing, lawyers for the media outlets said the president’s “ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
Ted Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly he should look past the administration’s new arguments that the ban was motivated by national security concerns and focus on what Trump has said about his decision.
“He is our lead witness here,” Boutrous said, pointing to Trump’s comments over the past several days that the outlets were too “negative.”
“He keeps proving our point,” Boutrous said.
Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” DOJ attorney Michael Velchik told the judge at the hearing.
He pointed to letters the White House press office sent to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” The letters also were filed in court.
The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia. Also cited was a Politico article about bad “vibes” at Republicans’ midterm convention.
In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
In the White House’s letter to Politico, it accused the outlet of violating professional standards, including by using anonymous sources. But one of the articles cited had been based on a press call that the White House hosted, according to an invitation reviewed by The Washington Post. The reporters on that call were told to cite an anonymous “senior administration official” in their reporting on the news, according to a recording reviewed by the Post.
Politico did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday evening.
Boutrous told the judge the letters were an attempt to manufacture rationale for the policy. Trump’s directive shows the result has been prejudged, he said.
“All of a sudden this is a national security issue” — a topic Trump didn’t mention at all when he announced and spoke about the ban on Friday, Boutrous added.
He urged the judge to let his clients get back to work. “These are urgent matters. We are at war,” the lawyer said.
Boutrous added that of the four CNN stories the White House complained about in its unsigned letter, only one was by a reporter who covers the building and has a hard pass that was renewed months after the story published.
Kelly questioned the government’s arguments. “I don’t know how a letter that they got after their pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of standards they would have to conform their conduct to,” the judge said.
He did not rule from the bench but said he’d take action “as soon” as he is able.
Ahead of the court hearing, more than four dozen media outlets and groups filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the judge to side with the banned outlets. NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, was among the groups in the brief.
The administration’s reason for the ban, the filing said, was “transparently viewpoint discriminatory.”
“The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene,” the group wrote in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.
In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.
The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” the court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”
“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.
MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool

A bitter battle over Dolly Parton’s legacy took a dramatic turn Tuesday when her longtime manager sought a restraining order against the country icon’s nephew.
Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, LLC, an entity Parton created to oversee her business interests, filed for a restraining order against Bryan Seaver in Nashville, according to The Associated Press.
Parton chose Seaver to publicly announce her death. The singer-songwriter died Aug. 25.
Less than a month later, a behind-the-scenes feud erupted into a legal battle.
DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY
Nozell and She's Alive accused Seaver of sending increasingly threatening messages in the weeks leading up to their request for a temporary restraining order. The filing came after She’s Alive fired Seaver over his alleged "terrorizing conduct."
Court documents obtained by The Associated Press show text messages and emails allegedly sent by Seaver.
The messages initially included threats to destroy the brand and, after Parton’s death, allegedly showed Seaver reveling in his newfound fame and calling himself an "international arms dealer."

In one message written Sept. 1 and included in the court documents, Seaver said, "I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f---ing pay me."
According to the court documents, the alleged messages rattled those within Parton’s business circle, leading several employees to resign and her trust and estate attorney to step away. She’s Alive also brought in private security to protect employees at work and at their homes.
She's Alive terminated Seaver Sept. 15 and asked the court to bar Parton's nephew from contacting or coming within 1,000 feet of its employees, attorneys and business partners.

Seaver pushed back against the allegations in a statement shared with TMZ.
"I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional, and I am a killer," he told the outlet. "However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats, and most of the comments I stand by."
He claimed the messages had been taken out of context to make them appear threatening.

"I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny, who I thought was my friend, and he fancies himself a gangster," he said. "A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
Fox News Digital has reached out to representatives for Nozell and Seaver for additional comment.

articles.title_orig: Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
articles.title_zh: Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
articles.content_orig:
Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford’s son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
-    Click here to listen to this article
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Detectives are trying to trace the supplier of the drugs that Cindy Crawford’s son, Persley Gerber, fatally overdosed on in Santa Monica rehab last weekend, according to law enforcement sources.
Gerber, 27, died at a luxury rehab center in Santa Monica on Sunday.
The Santa Monica Police Department said there is no indication of foul play at this time and that they are also investigating Gerber’s apparent overdose.
The sources told The Times the investigation is in its early stages.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s office conducted an autopsy Monday but deferred a cause and manner of death pending toxicology results for substances in Gerber’s system and that is expected to take several weeks, if not months, according to the office.
Gerber had entered the Resolution Living facility in Santa Monica just hours before his death, police said.
According to Resolution Living’s website, the house is a “Mental Health Recovery Residence.” The website describes it as part of a program that includes partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient treatment for a myriad of mental health issues, including depression, trauma and addiction, and offers dual diagnosis treatment for co-occurring disorders.
Santa Monica police received a call reporting a cardiac arrest and another call for an overdose at the center. Officers arrived at Resolutions Living, a $7.7-million, seven-bedroom mansion, at about 9:35 a.m. Sunday, a law enforcement source told The Times.
Resolutions Living did not return calls seeking comment.
It has become fairly common for police to now attempt to trace back the supplier of drugs in an overdose case.
Officials confirmed this week that Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl and other drugs, including a generic version of Xanax. Federal authorities probing her death are focusing their investigation in Los Angeles and are looking into whether the actor procured nonprescription pills from an area dealer. Drug Enforcement Administration agents and local investigators have questioned several people about the circumstances of her Aug. 16 death and have focused on her taking what was described as counterfeit pills before her demise.
The death of “Friends” star Matthew Perry sparked a sprawling drug investigation. Five people were charged with conspiracy to distribute ketamine to Perry, who died from acute effects of the drug.
Little is known about the Santa Monica police probe into Gerber’s death.
L.A. attorney Brian Claypool, who handles wrongful death litigation, said the autopsy and toxicology results “will be crucial in this tragic death to ascertain legal liability.”
Attorney Glen Jonas said depending on what police find, the rehab center could face scrutiny. Both attorneys said it is likely police will look closely at staffing, how the emergency was handled and other issues.
There have been cases in the past where drugs have been delivered into rehab centers.
The family of a Riverside woman sued a sober living center after she was found dead of a drug overdose.
In 2022, Edwin Oliva, of Montebello, was sentenced to over 33 years in federal prison for providing a lethal dose of fentanyl. During the early hours of Feb. 28, 2019, Oliva gave a woman a line of drugs to snort and did not tell her the substance was fentanyl — a powerful synthetic opioid. Believing the substance to be cocaine, the victim ingested the drug, which resulted in a fatal overdose.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein is sentenced to 15 years in prison for 2006 sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein is sentenced to 15 years in prison for 2006 sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein, the disgraced movie mogul, was sentenced in Manhattan to 15 years in prison Wednesday for a felony sex crime in another #MeToo reckoning.
Weinstein’s sentencing for sexually assaulting one-time TV production assistant Miriam Haley followed a legal odyssey spanning more than six years. His 2020 conviction was overturned by New York's highest court. A second jury found Weinstein guilty again at a retrial last year.
Once among the most powerful figures in the entertainment industry, Weinstein was an Oscar-winning producer whose hits included “Shakespeare in Love,” “Pulp Fiction” and “Chocolat.” But his downfall came quickly after sexual assault allegations in 2017 set off the #MeToo movement.
Weinstein, 74, is expected to appeal and maintains that he never raped or sexually assaulted anyone. He is now likely to remain behind bars well into his 80s. Seated in a wheelchair, he was quickly moved out of the courtroom after the sentencing, while some of his accusers hugged and brushed away tears.
Weinstein and his victim both spoke in court
Weinstein faced up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting Haley at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case cycled through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials, and again addressed the court Wednesday.
“Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come,” Haley said.
“It’s a life sentence for me,” she added.
Minutes later, Weinstein apologized while reiterating his innocence.
“Reflecting on all that has happened since 2017 has helped me recognize how my past conduct has negatively affected others. I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize to anyone I have affected with my actions,” he said.
Some of his accusers who were in court shook their heads while he spoke.
Weinstein is the face of MeToo, judge says
Judge Curtis Farber said Weinstein was once a king in the movie industry, “but recognition for these achievements will pale in comparison to what you did.”
He said Weinstein is now known as “a sexual predator, the literal face of the MeToo movement.”
The judge said Weinstein treated women as “mere objects to be played with and discarded” and still hasn’t accepted responsibility, portraying himself as a victim during jailhouse interviews.
Haley afterward said she was happy with the sentence, while saying it's clear that Weinstein has not acknowledged what he did. “I think he still feels entitled, and that’s part of the problem,” she said.
Haley’s lawyer, the famed victims’ rights attorney Gloria Allred, rejected any suggestion that Weinstein’s sentencing means the MeToo era is over.
“Women are empowered in a way they have never been before,” she said.
Why Weinstein is being sentenced a second time
Weinstein was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013.
Tried for a second time last year, he was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann.
After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again.
Weinstein’s health issues pushed the defense to ask for leniency
Defense lawyer Jacob Kaplan wanted three more years on top of the six years Weinstein already served, saying a longer sentence would make it more likely that Weinstein dies in prison.
Weinstein has been in the hospital six times since 2025, Kaplan said, while dealing with blood cancer, congestive heart failure, and kidney issues.
Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions — that were later thrown out — as an aggravating factor.
After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City’s notorious Rikers Island complex, Weinstein has been housed at a medical unit for inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan.
Haley describes the assault that led to Weinstein’s conviction
Haley, 49, is a former entertainment producer now working in advertising.
She said she met Weinstein through a mutual connection and worked briefly as a production assistant on “Project Runway,” a reality competition show that he produced.
Haley said she accepted an invitation to visit Weinstein’s apartment and after chatting briefly, he lunged to kiss her, she testified. She said she rebuffed him, but he grabbed her, forcibly backed her into a bedroom and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.
She recalled Weinstein asking, “Don’t you think we’re much closer now?” after either the alleged assault or a subsequent occasion when she says she had unwanted, but not forced, sex with him.
She also recalled telling him after the second encounter, “You know you can’t keep doing this.”
The Associated Press does not typically identify people who say they are victims of sexual assault unless they grant permission, which Haley, Sokola and Mann have done.

articles.title_orig: Iran’s president tells U.N. his country ‘must be powerful so as to avoid being threatened’
articles.title_zh: Iran’s president tells U.N. his country ‘must be powerful so as to avoid being threatened’
articles.content_orig:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital on Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of each other, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us," he said.
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faced a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now," he added,
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy.
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved," Taleblu said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Of course, the Trump administration is looking for a political win here," he concluded.

articles.title_orig: Iowa judge dismisses Trump’s lawsuit against Des Moines Register and pollster
articles.title_zh: Iowa judge dismisses Trump’s lawsuit against Des Moines Register and pollster
articles.content_orig:
A judge on Wednesday dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing the Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president’s claim that the newspaper’s poll coverage violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law.
Calling the case extraordinary, Scott J Beattie, the Iowa district judge, said that the argument could have a chilling effect that “can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs”.
He sided with pollster J Ann Selzer and the newspaper, who described the lawsuit as a conspiracy theory and an affront to free speech protections.
The ruling on Wednesday came hours after a judge heard arguments but did not rule from the bench in a case on Trump’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House grounds.
Beattie wrote that Trump’s suit sought to “stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability”.
After hearing the arguments, the judge concluded the constitutional protection “is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed.”
Trump and his team have filed several lawsuits against media organizations accusing them of bias, calling into question the boundaries of free speech protections, particularly for press. Some of those lawsuits have ended in settlements.
Trump filed the lawsuit against Selzer, the Des Moines Register and the newspaper’s parent company in December 2024, accusing them of fraudulently publishing inaccurate poll results to damage him and help Democrats, saying coverage of polls was not protected speech.
The judge made clear that the poll and coverage of it was constitutionally protected political speech and not a commercial product. He wrote that “allowing a legally faulty claim like this to proceed carries a cost that an ordinary case does not”.
Beattie said the case would have to be dismissed even if, solely for the purpose of deciding the motions, he accepted the Trump team’s allegations that the poll was intentionally skewed and its results fabricated. “Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails,” the judge wrote, adding that this was because the lawsuit did not meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks, the US representative, and Brad Zaun, the former Iowa state senator, both Republicans, joined the lawsuit. Selzer and her co-defendants wanted the case moved to federal court but, after a year of legal proceedings, the first hearing took place this year in state court.
The poll, conducted by Selzer’s company in the final days of October and released just days before election day 2024, showed then-vice president Kamala Harris, the Democrats’ presidential nominee, capturing 47% of Iowa likely voters, to Trump’s 44%.
Trump ultimately won the support of 56% of the nearly 2 million Iowans who voted.
Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations, valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and campaign funds and resources.
Selzer’s case was taken up by the free speech advocacy group the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. In separate filings, the Iowa pollster and the Register, with its parent company, Gannett Co, argued that courts had never considered polls or newspapers covering them to be commercial speech even though they may be sold for a profit.
They said the poll coverage, whether right or wrong in capturing the state of the race, was constitutionally protected political speech.
They also disputed the consumer fraud claim, emphasizing that the poll and coverage of it were not connected to transactions between the companies and Trump, Miller-Meeks or Zaun.

articles.title_orig: Boise's "Unknown Wanderer" is identified after 43 years. Could he be linked to Chicago Tylenol murders?
articles.title_zh: Boise's "Unknown Wanderer" is identified after 43 years. Could he be linked to Chicago Tylenol murders?
articles.content_orig:
Boise's "Unknown Wanderer" is identified after 43 years. Could he be linked to Chicago Tylenol murders?
Police in Boise, Idaho, announced Wednesday they had identified the "Unknown Wanderer," a man found dead in a church in 1982, and revealed a surprising possible connection to the still-unsolved Chicago Tylenol murders.
Investigators with the Ada County Sheriff's Office said they cannot place the man in the Chicago area during the final week of September 1982, when the poisonings happened, and they are not naming him as a suspect.
But they laid out a trail of evidence that includes a hand-drawn map of Chicago, photos of him in the Chicago area and a bottle of homemade cyanide. They have shared that evidence with Chicago police.
The mysterious death of a mysterious man
On Dec. 4, 1982, a man was found dead in Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise. He had no name and no identification. His wallet was empty, but sweat marks showed where cards had once been placed. He had an ink marker, a lighter, a Seiko wristwatch, a leather belt with a distinctive buckle, wore a bolo tie made with turquoise and silver, had two keyrings with nearly 30 keys between them and an envelope with $1,900 in $100 bills.
He also had a typed note signed William L. Toomey, which police determined had been a fake name.
His fingernails were finely filed, his hair dyed and styled, and his pants had either never been worn or were freshly pressed. He had a deep, even tan, the kind police said comes from living somewhere warm, and did not appear to have been living in the streets.
Investigators worked the case for years. His fingerprints did not match anything on file in Idaho or with the FBI. They traced his bolo tie to a silversmith in the Southwest, but that didn't produce a name. A 1990 episode of "Unsolved Mysteries" featuring the case generated thousands of tips but no real leads.
Ada County Sheriff Matt Clifford said detective Frank Richardson worked the case for decades until he retired. In 2019, Tim Cooper, a detective with 24 years on the job, reopened the case. He would be the one to find the break.
Key evidence: How they identified the wanderer
Cooper explained in a news conference Wednesday that while examining the nearly 30 keys that the wanderer had on him when his body was found, he discovered one that had a marking indicating it came from a hardware store in Jacksonville, Florida.
Cooper also spotted an etching on that key that had been previously misidentified and appeared to have been made with a sharp instrument.
Investigating the marking and etching led Cooper to a street in Jacksonville called Mills Court. He got the property deeds from the late 1970s and 1980s, and noticed that one property was owned by a man who had been reported dead in 1989. Cooper found his sole surviving family member, a brother living in Los Angeles, who confirmed his brother had lived in Jacksonville until he went missing in 1982, and had been declared dead in absentia years later.
Investigators compared the brother's DNA with DNA from the wallet and found a conclusive match showing the two men shared a father.
The Unknown Wanderer, Cooper said, was Dr. Mathew Francis Betkouski.
A privileged man with a preoccupation with poison
Betkouski came from a prominent Los Angeles family, investigators said. His grandfather had been president of the Los Angeles City Council and at times served as interim mayor. His father was a senior official with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
Betkouski had a documented fascination with chemistry and explosives from a young age and struggled with mental illness throughout his life, Cooper said. A traumatic brain injury in 1974 worsened his mental illness and caused "some of his problems to manifest in more concerning ways than they had before," Cooper said.
Betkouski moved to Jacksonville in 1975 to work for a flavors and fragrances company. Coworkers there reported him to management for talking about how to commit the perfect crime with poisons, and for talking about suicide, Cooper said.
Betkouski's paranoia grew more pronounced during that time, and coworkers sometimes saw him talking to himself, investigators said. In 1978, he returned to Los Angeles for two months of inpatient and outpatient mental health care. When he came back to Florida, he was fired from his Jacksonville jobs.
After his mother died in 1979, Betkouski spent more than a month in psychiatric treatment at a Florida state hospital, and likely at other places in the state, investigators said.
Betkouski's personal writings from those years show he was preoccupied with managing schizophrenia and depression, and with the possibility of achieving euphoria through "imaginary thoughts of violence."
In late 1979, Lockheed hired Betkouski to work at its test facility in White Sands, New Mexico. Fellow scientists there recalled him talking about how poison could be introduced into capsules of over-the-counter medication.
Police said Betkouski was fired from his Lockheed job in March 1982 after getting into an altercation at a local pharmacy where he allegedly attempted to get pills or capsules "for an experiment." When police were called, they discovered he had been conducting experiments in his home garden.
A link to the Chicago Tylenol murders?
In 2021, after Betkouski's brother died, his remaining relatives allowed Idaho police to go to Los Angeles, where they found personal items belonging to Betkouski his brother had kept in his childhood bedroom.
Among those effects were photos, letters and a hand-drawn map of Chicago that police believe was made in the 1970s. There was also a small bottle of cyanide with a handwritten label.
The bottle contained sodium cyanide, Cooper said, not the potassium cyanide used in the Chicago Tylenol poisonings. Testing found the bottle contained peach and apricot pits, leading police to believe the cyanide was homemade by Betkouski himself.
Police also said that writings from the late 1970s and early 1980s revealed Betkouski had an interest in visiting Chicago. Some of the photos found were of him in the Chicago area, which they initially thought were taken in late 1982 but were instead likely taken in December of 1981. Police are unsure if he returned to Chicago for subsequent trips after the photos were taken, and cannot place him there in the final week of September 1982, when the poisonings were carried out.
Boise police said they are not naming Betkouski as a suspect in the Chicago Tylenol murders because they cannot say for sure that he was there, but are still looking for further links between him and the Chicago area at that time.
They did note that he was found dead three months after the Tylenol murders, took steps to conceal his identity and the coroner ruled his cause of death as cyanide poisoning.
"While our office may have identified some connection to 1982 events, we're not naming him as a suspect," Detective Cooper said. "Our goal today is to general new leads to this case and possibly others."
Boise police said they have shared everything they learned that could be related to the Chicago Tylenol murders with the Chicago Police Department, which has reviewed their findings.
Chicago police released a statement, writing, "Chicago Police Department detectives have been in contact with the Ada County Sheriff's Office regarding its investigation to determine whether there is a connection to the Tylenol murders investigation, which remains an open cold case. Anyone with information that may assist in this investigation is asked to submit an anonymous tip through CPDTip.com or Cook County Crime Stoppers at 800-535-7867."
The Arlington Heights Police Department said it received and reviewed the information from the Ada County Sheriff's Office and would keep working with other agencies to identify "the individual or individuals responsible for the 1982 Tylenol murders." articles.title_orig: Giants QB Jaxson Dart will have knee surgery, ending his 2026 season
articles.title_zh: Giants QB Jaxson Dart will have knee surgery, ending his 2026 season
articles.content_orig:
Jaxson Dart's season is over.
The New York Giatns quarterback will undergo surgery and land on injured reserve after getting hurt during Monday night's 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, head coach John Harbaugh announced. While Dart is expected to make a full recovery, his 2026 season will be over.
According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, Dart's injury includes damage to his left MCL, PCL and meniscus. There is reportedly no ACL damage.
Harbaugh met with reporters on Tuesday afternoon and said that Dart was continuing to be evaluated and they had not made any decisions on the quarterback's status. The team "learned a lot more" about the injury following the MRI.
Harbaugh confirmed the injury on Wednesday afternoon. He did stop short of ruling Dart out for the postseason, should the Giants make the playoffs, but Dart will have surgery in the near future.
Dart suffered the injury in the first quarter on Monday night and did not return to the game. X-rays were negative and the second-year signal-caller underwent an MRI on Tuesday after the team returned home from Los Angeles.
During the game's opening drive, Dart dropped back to pass and jumped to make a throw downfield while under pressure. He was sandwiched between Rams linebackers Josaiah Stewart and Byron Young before falling to the ground holding his left knee.
Jaxson Dart is down on the field after this play. pic.twitter.com/R059M6kM6e
— TSN (@TSN_Sports) September 22, 2026
After being tended to on the field, Dart limped off and was taken for further evaluation. He was initially listed as questionable to return before being ruled out. He returned later without his uniform and watched the remainder of the game from the sideline.
Jameis Winston, who signed a two-year, $13-million extension before Week 1, finished the game going 11-for-27 with 111 passing yards, an interception and taking two sacks. Now, with Dart out for the year, Winston will presumably take the reins the rest of the way.
Jaxson Dart among Giants' MNF injury concerns
Dart wasn't the only injured Giant coming out of Monday night.
Wide receiver Malik Nabers injured his right shoulder in the first quarter. Nabers told reporters afterward that the shoulder popped out and he popped it back in, allowing him to return to the game the next series.
Linebacker Brian Burns had his left ankle rolled on by a Rams offensive lineman and needed help getting off the field. He limped his way to the Giants' locker room and was diagnosed with a low ankle sprain. He reportedly wore a boot on his left foot and while he said it's "nothing serious," it's unclear if Burns will miss any time.
Left tackle Andrew Thomas suffered a groin injury on the team's final offensive play, but no update has been provided on his status.
The Giants entered the game without cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo, who were ruled out due to injury.
The Giants' next two games are at home against the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals. They will go back on the road for Week 5 to face the Washington Commanders and return home for Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints. They will then travel to take on the Houston Texans before their bye in Week 8.

articles.title_orig: Tigrayan leaders say new war with Ethiopian government has begun
articles.title_zh: Tigrayan leaders say new war with Ethiopian government has begun
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.
The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
"It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media.
The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
The chairperson of the Africa Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and for both sides to resume talks.
The US ambassador to Ethiopia condemned the TPLF for making "the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive", describing it as an "unwinnable fight".
On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.
The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30.
"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.
Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.
He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.
But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.
On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.
It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.
It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.
In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.
Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.
There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.
