articles.title_orig: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
articles.title_zh: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
articles.content_orig:
Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".
The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.
Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.
The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".
The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.
Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.
Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.
Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.
Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.
"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.
"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."
Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.
The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.
A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.
A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games".
He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour.
"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games."
He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area".
FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league".
He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed."
A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined.
The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials.
The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games.

articles.title_orig: Eight sailors assigned to US carrier group that fought in Iran war attempted suicide, Navy secretary tells Congress
articles.title_zh: Eight sailors assigned to US carrier group that fought in Iran war attempted suicide, Navy secretary tells Congress
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story contains discussion of suicide. Help is available if you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters. In the US, call or text 988 for help. The International Association for Suicide Prevention and Befrienders Worldwide have contact information for crisis centers around the world.
Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a period that included when the ships undertook combat operations against Iran and the carrier set a modern record for its time at sea, according to a letter from the service’s acting secretary, which was obtained by CNN.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao revealed the number, which has not been previously reported and covers crew members from several ships that travel together, including the carrier, in written responses to questions posed by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew. Cao wrote that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment.
The rate of suicide attempts among the Lincoln strike group’s sailors was roughly consistent with that of the entire active duty Navy in 2024, the most recent year for which the Pentagon has released suicide data. That year, the Navy saw 356 suicide attempts among its estimated 337,000 active duty sailors.
“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote to Gillibrand, a Democrat and member of the Senate Armed Services, in a letter dated Tuesday. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.”
Between 6,000 and 7,000 US Navy sailors were deployed as part of the Lincoln strike group across roughly a half dozen ships — with the carrier kept out of port for over six months while conducting a high rate of combat operations against Iran.
“Eight attempted suicides is incredibly high,” one US military official told CNN, noting recent carrier strike group deployments have had one or two per year. “The strain of combat ops is much higher than normal deployments. No port calls, constant alerts, etc.”
The Navy did not respond ahead of publication to a request for comment about the letter.
The Lincoln deployed with various mental health resources onboard, including five chaplains, one embedded integrated prevention counselor, one psychologist, one clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and one expeditionary facility dog, according to Cao’s letter.
CNN previously reported that two sailors assigned to the Lincoln strike group, one from the carrier and one from another ship, had jumped overboard in recent months. Both were rescued, US officials said. Others were prevented from jumping, according to reports from the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.
In his letter to Gillibrand, Cao also confirmed that a sailor assigned to the airwing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered” and treated by the Lincoln’s medical department. “Additionally, one sailor attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to homeport.”
The Navy previously said in a statement to CNN, “We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”
A US official also previously told CNN that the Navy does not believe there is a correlation between deployment length and thoughts of self-harm, and that man overboard incidents are not unique to this group.
A crew member serving on the Lincoln previously described to CNN that morale on the carrier was very low and said they had heard repeatedly about suicidal ideation by fellow crew members. And there were regular strains on essential amenities — toilets and water fountains around the ship frequently closed, and hot water was often unavailable, the crew member said.
“Everyday we wake up and listen to our captain speak, we are desperately hoping and anxious for updates on our return,” the crew member, speaking before the ship had been ordered to return to its home port in San Diego, told CNN. The ship left the Middle East in August and is expected back in San Diego in the coming weeks.
Other sailors aboard the Lincoln who spoke with CNN described conditions unlike their prior deployments, largely due to the combat that has kept the carrier from making stops at friendly ports. Ships can take on new supplies and allow their sailors to rest and relax during those port calls.
CNN’s Davis Winkie contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Microsoft's New Surface Pro 12 And Surface Laptop 13 Feature Snapdragon X2 Plus Chips
articles.title_zh: Microsoft's New Surface Pro 12 And Surface Laptop 13 Feature Snapdragon X2 Plus Chips
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft's new Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 feature Snapdragon X2 Plus chips
There's also a new haptic Surface Mouse on the way.
Microsoft's hardware business seems to be in disarray on all fronts, especially Xbox, but it's still trucking along with refreshed versions of its smaller Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13. The big change is the new Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, which aims to be a solid update from the slower Qualcomm chips powering those devices last year. As Microsoft's smallest PCs, the key for both the Surface Pro 12 and Laptop 13 is portability over raw power. These were also ostensibly low-cost devices last year, with launch prices below $1,000, but as with everything else, the RAMaggedon has bumped the Surface Pro 12-inch up to $1,150 and the Surface Laptop 13 to $1,199.
Design-wise, nothing has changed with either device. The Surface Pro 12-inch is still a small 12-inch tablet with a kickstand, and it can transform into a pseudo-laptop with the $150 Surface Pro keyboard (sold separately, as always, because Microsoft seems to hate smart consumer choices). The Surface Laptop 13, meanwhile, is the company's basic notebook design shrunk down to a 13-inch screen and 2.7-pound frame. Both systems also feature new 500-nit displays, which are 25 percent brighter than before.
I thought the 12-inch tablet was absolutely adorable when I reviewed it last year, and I'm hoping the new internals alleviate my performance concerns. Microsoft claims the Snapdragon X2 Plus chips deliver 60 percent better graphics than the last generation, as well as 95 percent faster on-device AI and 18 percent better battery efficiency. As for basic Office productivity work, the company says the new chip is 18 percent faster. The upgrades sound compelling for anyone who was interested in these smaller Surface devices, but couldn't stomach the major speed downgrade of the previous Snapdragon X chips. If you picked up one of these systems last year, though, it's probably worth waiting a bit longer to upgrade. And if you need more power, the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and Surface Laptop 13.8-inch are also available with newer Snapdragon X2 chips (and much higher pricing of their own).
The Surface Pro 12-inch is also launching together with Microsoft Ink Canvas, an "AI-powered, pen-first experience for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the canvas," as the company describes. That doesn't sound particularly unique, but at least it's something to do with the Surface Slim Pen. The app will also be available on the Microsoft Store on October 13th for other Surface devices.
Alongside the PC hardware, Microsoft is launching a new $80 Surface Mouse, an ambidextrous mouse with haptic functionality. The company says you'll be able to feel certain Windows 11 interactions, like snapping a window or aligning objects. That's similar to what we've seen with the Logitech MX Master 4. It's an evolution of the previous Surface Mouse, which was notable for evoking Microsoft's classic Intellimouse design.
All of Microsoft's new Surface hardware will be available on October 13.

articles.title_orig: Seahawks' Macdonald apologizes to Broncos' Payton for comments
articles.title_zh: Seahawks' Macdonald apologizes to Broncos' Payton for comments
articles.content_orig:
The story of the day on Tuesday featured the unexpected disclosure of a behind-the-scenes beef between the Seahawks and Broncos. And while the whole thing was eye opening (and likely not intended for air), one specific line caught my eye.
Regarding Broncos coach Sean Payton’s assertion that the Seahawks had obtained training-camp footage through improper means, Macdonald said, “He thought it was a Michigan thing where we had a plant.”
That’s a reference to the 2023 Connor Stalions scandal in Ann Arbor, where Stalions developed a mechanism (in violation of NCAA rules) to scout future opponents with the goal of figuring out their sideline signals. In this specific context, Payton presumably suggested that the Seahawks sent someone to Broncos training camp to record their plays.
Beyond the fact that Macdonald’s journey included a year on Jim Harbaugh’s Michigan staff (2021, as defensive coordinator), the 2024 Seahawks employed former Michigan assistant Matt Weiss as an outside contractor. And while Weiss’s coaching career has imploded due to criminal allegations of widespread hacking, it’s fair to point out that the 2024 Seahawks had a distinct Michigan component.
That’s not to say Payton’s allegations had any merit. Faced with a threat that the Seahawks would sue the Broncos if Payton went public with his suspicions of shenanigans, the issue died. And it would have remained unknown if Macdonald had spoken about it into a hot mic.
It will be interesting to hear what Macdonald and Payton have to say about it today, when they meet with reporters for their usual Wednesday press conferences. Regardless of their likely efforts to downplay the situation and move on, the Seahawks have self-applied the kind of scarlet letter that will give the coaches of the teams they beat the same kind of excuse that plagued the Patriots during their run of dominance.
Pressed by owners as to why the Seahawks keep beating their teams, coaches can resort to the notion that the Seahawks cheat. Even without a shred of evidence to support that claim.
If/when that happens, it will trace to the fact that Macdonald got way too comfortable — and said way too much about a topic that otherwise would have never come to light.
Meanwhile, the Broncos host the Seahawks in 22 days, for a Thursday night game. Which will create a motivation for multiple media outles to fully explore the rabbit hole that, as of Tuesday morning, no one even knew existed.

articles.title_orig: Many voters see midterms as vote against Trump, new poll finds
articles.title_zh: Many voters see midterms as vote against Trump, new poll finds
articles.content_orig:
Many voters see midterms as vote against Trump, new poll finds
With less than six weeks until the November midterm elections, a plurality of American voters say their upcoming congressional vote will be "mainly a vote against President (Donald) Trump," according to a new Marist University poll.
In the NPR and PBS News-sponsored poll, released Sept. 23, 45% of registered voters described their midterm vote as primarily a "vote against President Trump than a vote for him."
A majority of independents, 54%, said their vote was "a vote against" the president, with an overwhelming majority of Democrats, 80%, sharing the same sentiment. Among Republicans, 35% said the president did not factor into their vote in November.
That plurality of voters coincides with a large Democratic lead in the generic congressional ballot. According to the newest poll, Democrats hold a lead of 12 percentage points over the GOP, up 2 points from the same poll in May.
According to Marist University, the poll was conducted among 1,280 respondents from Sept. 14 to Sept. 15 with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Democrats more trusted, poll shows
Voters’ rebuke of the president comes as his party looks to hold slim majorities in both the House and the Senate.
According to the poll, voters said they trusted Democrats over the GOP to manage the economy, foreign policy, gas prices, and, very narrowly, immigration. For immigration, 41% said they trusted Democrats while 38% gave Republicans the nod.
For Democrats, it is an 11-point improvement from 2024, when only 30% said they would do better than Republicans.
Voters’ trust in Democrats' handling of gas prices comes as the national average price of a gallon sits at $4.47, according to the AAA. That price marks an 11-cent jump from a week ago and a 38-cent increase from a month ago.
Trump approval staggers along
The September poll found Trump’s approval rating sitting at 39%, a 1-point improvement from its June poll. Despite the improvement, 53% of voters strongly disapproved of the president's job, which Marist University said shows an “electorate with hardened, high-intensity views rather than soft or persuadable ones.”
Trump’s approval rating in the new survey came on the heels of two bruising polls for the president.
On Sept. 22, a new Economist/YouGov poll found that his approval rating had fallen 5 points in a single week, from 40% to 35%, wiping out five straight weeks of gains in the same poll. That drop left the president just 2 points above the lowest rating he's ever recorded in the survey.
Then, a day before, on Sept. 21, an even worse poll saw Trump sink to the lowest approval rating of his political career in Reuters/Ipsos tracking. According to the poll, only 32% of Americans approved of Trump's job performance, a 3-point drop from the previous edition.
Trump’s 32% approval rating in the Sept. 21 poll set a new record low across both of his terms in office. Previously, Trump’s floor was 33%, which he reached in December 2017 and held for three consecutive weeks this August.
What do polling averages show?
While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to place Trump in negative territory overall:
- RealClearPolitics (Sept. 23): 39% approve, 59.5% disapprove
- New York Times (Sept. 23): 37% approve, 60% disapprove
- Silver Bulletin (Sept. 23): 37.6% approve, 59.9% disapprove
Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

McDonald’s to spend $8.5B on revamping restaurants, tech and franchise support
The multiyear plan is dubbed 'NEXT'
McDonald's on Wednesday announced new details as part of its long-term growth strategy, which will include a focus on upgrading restaurants and staff training, at an investor day at the corporate headquarters in Chicago.
The fast-food giant announced its NEXT growth and productivity strategy in June and outlined plans to implement changes throughout its system.
McDonald's said that to speed up the modernization of restaurants, deployment of technology and other operational improvements, it plans to provide about $8.5 billion in NEXT partnering support for franchisees through 2036, with roughly $5 billion provided through 2030.
The NEXT support for franchisees will include a combination of capital support and rent relief.
MCDONALD'S SAYS US SALES SLOWED AFTER VALUE DEAL PUSH FELL SHORT
The support comes with a target of about 250 basis points of gross restaurant-level efficiency improvements amounting to about $100,000 in annual cash flow benefits for the average restaurant, with the company saying the majority of that would benefit the restaurant's bottom line over time.
McDonald's announcement noted that the restaurant component of the plan aims to boost growth and productivity through simplified operations, elevated execution, modernized restaurant design and deploying generative AI-enabled ArchIQ at scale.
MCDONALD’S SHAKES UP FALL COFFEE LINEUP AS PUMPKIN SPICE SEASON HEATS UP
The company also announced a multiyear training program called "Make it Golden" that will begin on Founder's Day, Oct. 5, which aims to improve customer service to create more consistency for patrons and increase repeat visits.
"McDonald's has the unmatched scale, customer insights, brand loyalty, and operational capabilities to not only adapt to the next wave of change in our industry, but to turn it into an advantage," said McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski. "That's what McDonald's > NEXT is about: to be the first choice for more customers, more often – while making our restaurants stronger and easier to run."
MCDONALD'S SERVING UP NEW KIND OF ENERGY BOOST ON MENUS NATIONWIDE
"We are confident that executing across the key components of NEXT will unlock stronger restaurant economics, generate attractive returns for the Company, our franchisees and shareholders, and increase capacity to keep investing in growth," Kempczinski added.
McDonald's announcement also included new market share targets, calling for 1.5 percentage points of growth in both chicken and beverages by 2030, while also maintaining the company's leadership in beef market share.

Sales growth from unit expansion is also targeted to contribute nearly 2.5% to system-wide sales growth in 2027, moderating to about 2% by 2030.

articles.title_orig: FBI investigates breach of jobs website as hackers claim ‘very sensitive data’ stolen
articles.title_zh: FBI investigates breach of jobs website as hackers claim ‘very sensitive data’ stolen
articles.content_orig:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its jobs website as a criminal hacking group claimed to have accessed “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants.
“The FBI is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating,” the bureau said in a statement. The website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline Wednesday morning.
A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack.
The message, directed to FBI director Kash Patel as well as the assistant director in charge of the FBI’s cyber division, said the hacking group had “compromised very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job”.
The claims could not immediately be verified, and an FBI spokesperson declined to comment further. An email to an address associated with the organization was not immediately returned.
In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations in an FBI public service announcement from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion”.
That announcement characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often “use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims”, commonly harass or threaten victims and “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist”.
ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was “offended” by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims.
The FBI has been a common hacking target.
In March, the agency disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel’s and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work résumé and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.

articles.title_orig: Draft analyst Jeremiah: Marvin Harrison Jr. is unrecognizable with Cardinals
articles.title_zh: Draft analyst Jeremiah: Marvin Harrison Jr. is unrecognizable with Cardinals
articles.content_orig:
Draft analyst Jeremiah: Marvin Harrison Jr. is unrecognizable with Cardinals
Marvin Harrison Jr's rapid decline since the NFL Draft is puzzling to evaluators.
NFL Network analyst Daniel Jeremiah told Seattle Sports that Marvin Harrison Jr., the can’t-miss prospect he evaluated at Ohio State, is unrecognizable as an Arizona Cardinal.
“I don’t even recognize Marvin Harrison Jr. from the guy I watched in college,” Jeremiah said.
The scout goes on to speak rather definitively on how Harrison not only needs a change of scenery, but that it might not even work elsewhere.
“I don’t have all the information to know what has gone on there,” he said. “He’s obviously going to have to go somewhere else but I’m not even confident that a fresh start and a new place is going to unlock him. He looks sluggish, he doesn’t look like he can separate.”
Harrison has one catch for 33 yards through two games. While his first two seasons since going fourth overall in the 2024 NFL Draft weren’t pacing that poorly, it still was nowhere close to the level of being the nearly-guaranteed star wideout he was evaluated to be in the draft by experts like Jeremiah.
Jeremiah went on to say that of the Buckeyes’ plethora of high-tier wideout prospects over a short span, he would have had Harrison ranked ahead of Chris Olave, Garrett Wilson and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Since those drafts, though, he says it’s clear that Harrison is the worst of the four.
Harrison had a handful of all-22 clips from Sunday’s catch-less loss go viral on social media, including a few run-blocking scenarios in which a lack of effort is clear.
“I just don’t see it that way,” Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said when asked if Harrison is not exerting maximum effort. “I think his running style is different than some other people. If that’s people’s narrative on him, that’s fine. I know his teammates don’t feel that way.”
This has led to trade speculation, which ESPN’s Dan Graziano said naturally spawned dialogue from opposing front offices on if Harrison could indeed be made available by Arizona. Harrison will be under contract for at least one more season beyond 2026. The Cardinals, however, will have to decide on his fifth-year option next offseason, and if this trend continues, they will surely decline that.

articles.title_orig: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
articles.title_zh: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft.
According to official documents, between $6.5m (£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000.
Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows.
A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties.
The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.
"There are no conflicts of interest."
According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency.
SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June.
Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut.
Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump.
Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year.
The disclosure of the July trades made on behalf of Trump emerged against a backdrop of renewed focus on AI and how safe it is.
Trump has rejected calls for safety-driven slowdowns, warning that restrictions risk the US slipping behind China.
He told an audience of world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that he wants to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" to project American dominance.
Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, stating last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins."
He is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails, putting him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN, including Secretary General António Guterres who continues to advocate for binding international safeguards.
The president is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week during a state visit to Washington.
While Trump frames a rebrand as an instrument of national competition, his administration is simultaneously proposing an emergency AI "hotline" with Beijing to manage potential cyber risks or rogue AI incidents.

articles.title_orig: ‘Dancing With the Stars’: Emma Slater Reacts to Boyfriend Alan & Giada’s Elimination
articles.title_zh: ‘Dancing With the Stars’: Emma Slater Reacts to Boyfriend Alan & Giada’s Elimination
articles.content_orig:
‘Dancing With the Stars’: Emma Slater Reacts to Boyfriend Alan & Giada’s Elimination
- Giada De Laurentiis and Alan Bersten were voted off Dancing With the Stars on September 22.
- After the episode, fellow contestant Tatyana Ali and Bersten’s girlfriend, Emma Slater, opened up to TV Insider about the elimination.
- Slater admitted that she’s excited to have Bersten help her in the studio now that he’s gone home.
The kitchen closed for Giada De Laurentiis and her pro partner Alan Bersten when the two were eliminated from the September 22 episode of Dancing With the Stars. The pair danced a salsa to Becky G‘s song “Bella Ciao,” which translates, ironically, to “Goodbye, Beautiful.”
The key to lasting on DWTS is to improve one’s performance from the previous week. De Laurentiis and Bersten scored 16 points in the show’s premiere week, performing a tango to” Venus.” This week, the duo dropped four points, earning a score of 12 for their salsa.
Tatyana Ali (The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air), paired with Jan Ravnik, told TV Insider right after the live show on Tuesday that she and De Laurentiis had bonded during their short time together in the competition.
“She’s just as lovely as I imagined her to be,” Ali said, fondly. “I’ve been a fan of hers, especially last week, when our scores came in and they were both really low. She took the time to come over to me and just kick it with us on the balcony. She’s a really special lady and I’m going to miss her.”
Meanwhile, Bersten’s girlfriend, pro Emma Slater, said she’s “really sad” to see the pair go home. “I don’t want to see anybody go, but, of course, Alan, specifically, and Giada is such a beautiful person,” she admitted. “I voted for her tonight! I voted for her last week, too. I think she is wonderful, and I wish that her journey here on the show could continue.”
She added, “I know Alan feels really proud of her.” However, now Bersten can more freely offer his time and support in helping Slater’s quest for Mirrorball gold with her partner, Jackson Olson, of the Savannah Bananas.
“[Alan] will most likely come and help me,” a grateful Slater mused. “And I welcome his support because he’s got such a great eye for choreography.”
Olson and Slater have one of the more grueling travel and rehearsal schedules this season as he continues to perform with his fellow Savannah Bananas. This weekend, the Bananas are competing against the Texas Tailgaters in Arlington, Texas.
“We’ve basically given our lives to this,” Olson enthused. “Not just the dancing, not just the baseball, and not just the TikToks and content, but everything’s encapsulated into one. Both of our work ethics have shown that we [want] to win this thing. We’re going to have that work ethic every single day, not matter what the travel, the red-eyes, canceled flights, and delayed flights – all of it!”
While the travel and performance schedule is demanding, Olson and Slater, by staying in the front of baseball audiences, may be picking up a lot of votes. “The ‘Banana’ fans are so awesome, and they really have our backs with everything,” Olson gushed. “They want us to do well, and I think that they’re going to be an integral part of what we do.”
Olson already feels like a winner by being partnered with Slater. “When I walked in my first day and I saw Emma, I was immediately like, ‘Alright!'” he confirmed. “I had in my head all the ideas for the TikToks I wanted to make. I also know that Emma is a badass choreographer. I remember seeing last year how she turned Andy [Richter] into a dancer.”
Slater told Olson that he’s well on his way to becoming just that. “You are becoming a dancer,” Slater informed her celebrity partner during this interview. “Just with the one-week improvement, I really feel that you are becoming that.”

articles.title_orig: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.
Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Greets Xi for State Visit Amid U.S.-China Tensions: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Trump Greets Xi for State Visit Amid U.S.-China Tensions: Live Updates
articles.content_orig: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. At the same time, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning the outlets from the White House. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington this evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. And at the same time, a federal judge today heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning them from the White House. Our Liz Landers is at the White House covering both stories, and she joins us now. So, Liz, we will start with this state visit. What is the focus of it? Liz Landers: Yes, Geoff, President Trump is greeting leader Xi right now at Joint Base Andrews here in Washington for an arrival ceremony that has all the pomp and circumstance of this major state visit. This is the first time that Xi has been to the White House since 2015. And President Trump visited China back in May and was not awarded this same kind of pomp, circumstance and arrival. In particular, Xi did not greet him when he landed there in China back in May. You're seeing some of those images now. I will remind our viewers that those images are from several months ago because the White House TV pool is still not covering the president's events today. We believe that there are going to be a number of issues that will be addressed during this visit. A senior administration official told us earlier that AI, artificial intelligence, of course, will be on the top of the list, also some of these export controls that the United States has on our computing chips and selling those to China. The possibility of reducing tariffs on some goods is apparently going to come up, and also political prisoners. Several China watchers and experts that I have spoken with don't really think that this meeting is going to be so much about deliverables as it is about continuing to forge that personal relationship that President Trump has with leader Xi. I spoke earlier today with Kyle Chan. He's a fellow at the Brookings institute. And he was actually talking about these export controls, saying that matters less and less for the Chinese government because they are going all out to build their own AI chips themselves. And when it comes to artificial intelligence in particular, you heard some of that addressed from the U.N. today in Nick's story. China is not interested in a joint slowdown of AI development, according to Chan. He says that they're more worried about cyber risks, hacking companies, and they don't share, China does not share the same concerns that we have heard from U.S. AI companies and leaders recently that robots, AI may kill us all in the near future. Geoff, one more thing I want to add. Not everybody is happy about this visit and all of the accoutrements that are being laid out for President Xi. Republican Senator Wicker, he's the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, says that he would have advised against this lavish welcome to what he calls a brutal dictator. Geoff Bennett: And, Liz, there's a state dinner tomorrow evening. Who is expected to be in attendance? Liz Landers: Well, Geoff, as you would imagine, with all of this talk of AI and technology, there are leaders from several major business companies and AI companies that are going to be at the White House tomorrow. A senior administration official says that Jeff Bezos will be there, as well as Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, a chipmaker, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. The first lady, Melania Trump, said in a FOX News interview today that President Trump wanted to have the state dinner because they have a great relationship. She said that she's been involved in every detail of the planning for the state dinner tomorrow night. And she also -- and I'd also just add that this is only the second state dinner that President Trump has now had in his second term in office, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz, in the minute we have left, bring us up to speed on this lawsuit involving the three news organizations that were banned from the White House by President Trump. Liz Landers: There was a hearing on this, this afternoon, and the judge in this case, a district judge here in Washington, said right off the bat that he was skeptical of the argument that the Trump administration, that the Trump White House is making here on due process grounds. It sounds like the judge believes that the due process of these news organizations was violated. The government is arguing in a filing that they issued late last night that news organizations failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House. This has now turned into a conversation about national security. That is what the president and the administration are arguing is at stake here, that these news organizations somehow violated national security there. The judge also seemed skeptical of that, Geoff. We still do not have an answer from the judge as to whether the ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW will be lifted. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers outside the West Wing at the White House for us tonight. Liz, thanks so much. Liz Landers: Of course.

articles.title_zh: Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
articles.content_orig:
Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
Washington — President Trump is offering a warm welcome to Chinese President Xi Jinping this week as the U.S. tries to choke China's supply of semiconductor chips for artificial intelligence advancement, as the two countries determine whether their fragile truce on tariffs will continue, and as concerns mount about China's relationships with Iran and Russia.
Xi's visit to the White House, the first in more than a decade, features a state arrival ceremony Wednesday, with Mr. Trump taking part along with U.S. military personnel.
Thursday will bring a formal meeting of the two presidents and a state dinner. Xi's wife, Peng Liyuan, is joining the trip.
Mr. Trump and Xi last met in May, when Xi welcomed the U.S. president for a state visit in Beijing.
What to expect on the schedule
Mr. Trump welcomed Xi and his wife at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday, a rare instance of a sitting president greeting a foreign leader on the tarmac instead of awaiting them at the White House.
A military band played as Xi and his wife exited a massive Air China jet while the American president and first lady awaited them on a red carpet at the bottom of the stairs. The arrival ceremony, which included a flyover with two B-1 bombers, was quick, and Mr. Trump and the first lady departed about 10 minutes later.
On Thursday morning, the president and first lady Melania Trump will host another arrival ceremony for Xi and his wife on the White House South Lawn. The White House says the ceremony will feature nearly 500 service members from all branches of the U.S. military.
The U.S. and Chinese flags will be displayed on the South Portico, according to the White House. The U.S. Marine Band will play the anthems of both the U.S. and China, the White House says. Then, both Mr. Trump and Xi are expected to speak.
The arrival ceremony is also expected to have a military flyover with a B-2 Spirit bomber and four F-22s.
The presidents' spouses are expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday while Mr. Trump and Xi meet. A state dinner will be Thursday evening.
On Friday, the couples will have tea at the White House before heading to the National Archives. The visit will then conclude.
China experts say not to expect many big policy achievements
China experts say to not expect many tangible policy outcomes from the meeting. James Lewis, a distinguished fellow with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, said there "isn't much of a formal agenda" for the two leaders.
"I'm not anticipating very much — I don't think anyone is," Lewis said. "Because this is largely for show. And it's largely a discussion between two very cautious and two very suspicious leaders."
"I don't think there's too much hope for policy achievements," said Jake Werner, director of the East Asia Program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
"Probably more than anything, Trump loves a show," Werner added. "He loves to put on a show. And secondarily, he thinks he has a relationship with Xi Jinping, who he thinks is a big, strong man, and he values those sorts of relationships. And then I think … he has a desire to make sure that China doesn't use the power that it demonstrated that it has last year when it cut the U.S. off of rare-earth elements, and American factories started shutting down."
Mr. Trump has often praised Xi and cast his warm personal relationship with the Chinese leader as an asset. During his visit to Beijing earlier this year, Mr. Trump called Xi a "great leader" and said the two men have always been able to work out their disagreements.
As for the disagreements that could dominate this week's visit: This is the meeting of the three "Ts," as Lewis put it — trade, tech and Taiwan.
What Trump and Xi may discuss on tariffs and trade
On trade, the U.S. and China will have to decide whether to extend a truce on tariffs that expires on Nov. 10.
That deal, struck in Busan, South Korea, in October, lowered tariffs levied by both countries and paused restrictions on Chinese exports of rare earth minerals. It also said China would continue to buy large quantities of U.S. soybeans, a pledge China has failed to keep.
The truce allowed the two countries to climb down from a tit-for-tat trade war that sent U.S. and Chinese tariffs to more than 100% at one point in spring 2025.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend, said the Chinese have proposed a "bigger deal" on trade between the U.S. and China, beyond the trade truce brokered in Busan, South Korea, in October.
Bessent said Mr. Trump and Xi may meet "up to four times" this year, so they're open to different approaches. Thursday will be their second meeting.
"We're open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement, or examining the bigger deal," Bessent told reporters Wednesday. "We're fine with both, and we're going to do what's best for the American people."
On Fox News Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there will be an announcement establishing a U.S.-China "Board of Trade," which will determine a "relatively small subset of goods" that the two countries agree they should protect from trade disputes. That may include things like low-tech consumer goods and some agricultural products, Greer said. The idea of such a board was discussed when Mr. Trump and Xi met in May.
Trump and Xi may discuss artificial intelligence
Amid growing public pressure for the U.S. government to implement more safeguards around advanced artificial intelligence, Bessent shared over the weekend that the U.S. has proposed a new "notification system" alerting AI incidents that affect national security. He made the announcement following a meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
"We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats," Bessent said, according to the Associated Press. "We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important."
It's not yet clear if Mr. Trump is on board with that idea. His most-voiced concern about AI is the need for the U.S. to beat China, and he has spoken out against the idea of reining in the speed of AI research. He slowed and altered an executive order allowing the government to voluntarily review the latest frontier AI models before they are released.
Lewis said Xi wants access to advanced computer chips and to be able to sell memory chips to the U.S. Nvidia, one of the leading designers of the chips that power AI models, is currently prohibited from selling its most advanced products in China, though Mr. Trump has allowed it to sell its H200 chips to "approved customers."
There is also growing concern that Chinese AI developers are using a method called "distillation" to train Chinese AI models based on U.S. frontier models, according to the federal government's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
AI is on the Trump-Xi agenda, a White House official told reporters on a call Friday on the condition of anonymity, although the person didn't elaborate. A reporter asked the White House official if the president will have a substantive call with Xi about AI safety, and if Mr. Trump is prepared to extend or renew the existing semiconductor chip-related licenses with China.
"Those are both on the agenda, both AI and the current 'Busan' truce, and we'll know more once the two leaders meet," the White House official said.
Taiwan is a key issue for Xi
Beijing is looking to reclaim Taiwan and wants the U.S. to stay out of the way, Lewis said. The U.S. has a multibillion-dollar deal to sell arms to Taiwan, and "the Chinese hate that," Lewis said.

articles.title_orig: Future of Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute uncertain
articles.title_zh: Future of Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute uncertain
articles.content_orig:
The Department of the Air Force is shutting down its premier think tank dedicated to studying Chinese aerospace, despite previously saying it would only cut civilian roles, according to the organization’s director.
On Tuesday, an Air Force spokesperson told Federal News Network that the service would no longer assign civilian positions to the China Aerospace Studies Institute as a part of the ongoing civilian restructure within Air Education and Training Command.
The spokesperson, however, did not confirm the assertion that CASI is shutting down, saying instead that the “mission continues with the organization leveraging assigned military service members to accomplish its objectives.”
“The China Aerospace Studies Institute is not closing,” the spokesperson said. “Air University continues to evaluate the alignment of the CASI mission to best support DAF priorities.”
“Civilian employees affected by this restructure will continue in their current positions until further notice and will be evaluated for reassignment,” the spokesperson added.
CASI’s official X account later published a statement that “Air University has decided to close the China Aerospace Studies Institute.”
Brendan Mulvaney, the organization’s director, said that all of CASI’s billets will go into an unfunded status beginning Oct. 1.
“That doesn’t mean we are going to cease operations right on the first of October. CASI has commitments that it has made and will honor, to the best of our ability, through at least March of 2027,” Mulvaney, who has been the center’s director since 2017, said in a statement.
“What it does mean is that the amazing team of researchers and scholars at CASI are going to have to start to look for new positions elsewhere. Rest assured, CASI employees will continue to work and get paid while in a ‘surplus’ status (meaning they remain employed and paid while we help them find new positions), and I will do my best to make sure they all land someplace that will truly appreciate their talents… As time goes on, unless we find a new home within the Department for the whole CASI team, I expect people to find other jobs and move on. Once all of the civilians eventually depart, CASI will close,” he added.
The Air Force spokesperson said that eight civilian positions have been impacted by the service’s 2026 civilian workforce optimization effort.
“Employees filling those positions will continue to serve and support CASI alongside five military members for the foreseeable future,” the spokesperson said.
CASI opened its doors in 2017 to study China’s air and space capabilities. The organization’s unclassified research informs policy and strategy across the Defense Department and broader U.S. government.
The defense community called the Air Force’s decision to “shutter” CASI “extremely unfortunate and regrettable,” describing the center as “the most prolific producer of publicly-accessible open source research about [the People’s Liberation Army] in the United States.”
“CASI has measurably increased knowledge about the PLA within the U.S. government, academia, think tanks and the broader public, which should be in the U.S. government’s interest, given that strategic competition with the PRC is the most important,” Will Yale, a Navy surface warfare officer, said on social media platform X.
Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said it is a “truly incomprehensible decision and a devastating loss for the analytic community.”
Workforce cuts at CASI are part of the Defense Department’s ongoing efforts to restructure its civilian workforce — the department eliminated approximately 78,000 civilian positions in 2025.
If you would like to contact this reporter about recent changes in the federal government, please email anastasia.obis@federalnewsnetwork.com or reach out on Signal at (301) 830-2747.

articles.content_orig:
Trump rolls out the red carpet for China's Xi
Bessent says the trade truce between the two countries is extended to Jan. 10.
President Trump rolled out the red carpet for President Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening at Joint Base Andrews, joined by the first lady to personally welcome the Chinese president and his wife, Madame Peng Liyuan, to the United States for their high-stakes, three-day visit.
The two leaders are expected to discuss a number of issues, including artificial intelligence safety, Taiwan, trade, the war in Iran and critical minerals.
Trump and his motorcade rolled near the edge of the red carpet then the pomp and circumstance began.
The president and the first lady held hands and walked to the foot of the stairs in front of Xi's plane, standing for a few moments before the Chinese leader and Madame Peng descended.
The U.S. Air Force band began playing but paused as the leaders mingled at the bottom of the stairs.
Xi shook hands with some Chinese officials before the couples walked down the red carpet, lined with U.S. service members. They stood for a photo opportunity at the bottom of the carpet, the Air Force band starting to play again, and cannons went off. The Chinese anthem played first, then Trump saluted during "The Star Spangled Banner."
Two B1 bombers flew low over the leaders.
The leaders and their spouses exchanged a few more pleasantries before Xi and Madame Peng got into their car and Trump and the first lady walked over his motorcade moments later. Neither Trump nor Xi made remarks.
Speaking to reporters after landing back at the White House, Trump said he would discuss Iran during Xi's visit.
"We'll see. We'll see. I'll be talking about that and many other subjects. We'll see, but it's all coming along well, including that," Trump said, when asked if he and Xi would address Iran.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday evening that the U.S. and China reached an agreement to extend their trade truce until Jan. 10.
"We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement. The detente -- economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10, that is going to be extended until Jan. 10, to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front," Bessent told Fox News.
Asked if he thinks the Chinese are seeking a bigger deal now that there's more time to hash out specifics, Bessent said he didn't know if that was possible.
"I don't know whether a bigger deal can be done. I don't know whether we will just roll the current deal," he told Fox. "There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side so we also want to see -- now that we've sat down and told them our expectations, to see if over the coming months, they could be a bit more fulsome in enacting the agreement."
The airport greeting was unusual for Trump and reflects the pomp and circumstance surrounding the visit as Trump traditionally greets foreign leaders at the White House.
He'll do that on Thursday when he and first lady Melania Trump welcome Xi and his wife at a ceremony on the State Floor of the White House. Trump and Xi will also participate in a review of troops in the Rose Garden before they head into formal, private talks.
Following that, Xi and his wife will be the guests of honor when Trump and the first lady host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the East Room, where both leaders are expected to deliver remarks.
Guests scheduled to attend the state dinner include tech executives like Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai of Google and Michael Dell, the CEO of Dell Technologies, the White House and a source familiar told ABC News.
Also on the guest list are Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup, and Tim Cook, who recently stepped down as the CEO of Apple.
On Friday, Xi and his wife are scheduled to join Trump and the first lady for a private tea and a tour of the National Archives to view historical national documents. Xi is expected to depart the U.S. later Friday.
Xi's last state visit to the U.S. was in September 2015 during the Obama administration. Trump visited China last May for talks with Xi.
ABC News' Emily Chang contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: US, China agree to extend 'the Busan agreement' until January, Bessent says
articles.title_zh: US, China agree to extend 'the Busan agreement' until January, Bessent says
articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have agreed to extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire in November through Jan. 10, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday.
The announcement came after Bessent and China’s vice premier, He Lifeng, held an unscheduled meeting in Washington.
“We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement’ — the economic détente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 — that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said in an interview on Fox News Channel.
Bessent said it’s possible a larger economic package will be agreed upon by January. But it’s also possible to “just roll the current deal” and extend it further.
“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations, if over the coming months they can be more fulsome in enacting the agreement,” he said.
The announcement, a big win for economic stability in both countries, came only minutes after Chinese President Xi Jinping touched down to begin a multiday state visit to Washington.
Bessent also indicated that there could be further announcements in coming days from the Chinese delegation, including agreements to buy more American agricultural products and potential deals in the financial services sector.
Since Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have been holding talks with their Chinese counterparts to lay the groundwork for the closely watched state visit.
On Sunday, Bessent and Greer announced that the U.S. and China had proposed exchanging alerts about AI-related hacking incidents, especially those that concern national security.
The U.S. and China could also agree on lists of goods on which lower tariffs would be applied as part of President Donald Trump’s “Board of Trade” initiative with China, Greer told reporters.
“We expect that the types of goods you’ll see in those lists are consumer goods, low-tech items coming in from the Chinese side,” he said. “On the U.S. side, energy products, agricultural goods, potentially medical devices and other things like that.”
Xi’s visit is his first trip to the U.S. in more than a decade.
News of the trade truce extension is likely to be widely welcomed in Washington and Beijing, given that the U.S. and China are vital sources of goods for each other and for their millions of consumers and businesses.

articles.title_orig: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in United States for state visit
articles.title_zh: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in United States for state visit
articles.content_orig:
Sept. 23 (UPI) -- U.S. President Donald Trump greeted President Xi Jinping of China on Wednesday evening as the Chinese leader arrived at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, marking the start of a three-day state visit.
The tarmac greeting was a rare gesture for an incumbent U.S. president to a foreign leader. Trump and first lady Melania Trump met Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on a red carpet as the U.S. Air Force band performed the countries' national anthems. The ceremony also included a cannon salute, a 21-person honor cordon, color guards and a flyover by two B1 bombers.
There will be another ceremony Thursday morning at the White House featuring more than 500 U.S. service members. The presidents will meet Thursday afternoon with a state dinner Thursday night.
Both Republicans and Democrats have criticized the visit and the lavishness of Trump's treatment of the Chinese leader, The Hill reported . Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said onthe Senate floor Tuesday that Trump should remember that Xi "is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."
A statement by a group of Senate Democrats including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also criticized Trump's red-carpet treatment of the Chinese leader.
"President Xi gets the royal treatment while President Trump hurls threats and wages trade wars on allies like Canada," they wrote. "This is not leadership, and Americans deserve better."
The Democrats called on Trump to end China's access "to the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment it needs to build dangerous AI systems," stand with Taiwan against China and press Xi to stop supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
The trip marks XI's first state visit to the United States in 11 years.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Trump welcomes Xi for state visit as US-China trade truce to be extended
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Trump welcomes Xi for state visit as US-China trade truce to be extended
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has spent years trying to squeeze China — imposing tariffs, cutting off access to advanced technology and pressing U.S. allies to reduce their dependence on Beijing. When he begins meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, he'll juxtapose the long-standing bluster with the pomp and circumstance the leaders lavish on each other.
The pageantry began immediately. Upon arrival at Maryland's Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening, Xi and Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan were greeted by Trump, First Lady Melania Trump and a swarm of U.S. service members, some of whom rolled out a large red carpet for the visiting leader.
Before leaving the tarmac, Xi was treated to a flyover during a rendition of the U.S. national anthem.
The two-day tête-à-tête will take place as Trump confronts a China that has proved harder to isolate and allies increasingly reluctant to line up behind the U.S. to do it.
Part of that is Beijing's doing. China has deepened trade ties around the world while building leverage of its own, most notably through rare earths. Its global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year, reaching a record $1.2 trillion for 2025 even as its exports to the U.S. dropped.
But the shift also reflects Trump's approach. Since returning to office, fights over tariffs, defense spending and personal spats have strained relationships with traditional allies even as Trump has pursued a more transactional relationship with Xi.
Countries Washington has traditionally counted on to magnify its power are increasingly seeking room to maneuver between the world's two largest economies.
As a result, Trump enters Thursday's summit facing a test of whether strains with U.S. allies have made it harder to marshal American power against Xi.
"China is presenting itself to the world as the stable counterweight to an erratic and violent United States," said Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution think tank. "America retains unmatched power on the world stage, but leverage requires a united front and there are a shrinking number of countries willing to follow America's lead right now."
For decades, one of the U.S.'s biggest advantages over China has been its network of allies and partners. When the U.S. restricted technology or imposed sanctions, bringing major economies in Europe and Asia along made those measures harder for Beijing to evade.
China still lacks anything comparable: The Lowy Institute, an independent Australian foreign-policy think tank, scored the U.S. defense networks at 81.4 on a scale of 100, versus 18.9 for China in 2025. But Beijing does not need U.S. allies to switch sides to erode that advantage. It only needs them to become less willing to move with Washington, Hass and other China experts said.
"When democratic countries don't have public support for a counterpart, it raises the cost for leaders to align with the United States," Hass told CNBC. "It lowers the cost for leaders to defy the United States."
Trump has taken a sledgehammer to relationships with allies. He's clashed with NATO over defense spending, threatened to reduce the U.S. troop presence in much of Europe while announcing plans Tuesday to add troops in Greenland after threatening to take over the island and imposed tariffs on the U.S.'s northern neighbor Canada.
"Although our biggest economic complaints regarding China's economy are shared by many of our allies and partners, the current U.S. approach is to attack all of those countries ... instead of forming a common front," said Melanie Hart, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
Meanwhile, public confidence in the U.S. as a reliable partner has fallen. In Canada, the share of people who described the U.S. as a reliable partner fell from 83% in 2022 to 35% this year, according to Pew Research Center in June. In Germany, the share who said Washington considers other countries' interests when making foreign policy fell from 60% in 2023 to 23%.
Canada this month was invited to be the first "associate member" of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government seeks deeper defense ties with Europe and less reliance on the U.S.
Foreign allies "worry that as soon as they make a deal with us, Washington will undercut them in some way that they will then regret," Hart told CNBC.
China has sought to capitalize on that opening, not necessarily by persuading countries to choose Beijing over Washington, but by making the choice less binary.
The country remains a U.S. security partner and a strategic competitor of China, with troops from both countries still deployed along their disputed Himalayan border. Yet Xi visited India this month for the first time in seven years as the two countries took what Tanvi Madan, a senior fellow at Brookings, called "baby steps" toward stabilizing relations.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese data, and Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to strengthen business and transport links despite unresolved security disputes.
"Uncertainty over Trump's approach to Beijing and strains in India's own relationship with the U.S. have given India another reason to keep relations with China on steadier ground," Madan told CNBC. "Even a tactical détente between the U.S., India and China can have downstream impacts on India's strategic environment."
The changing balance of leverage is most tangible in the economic relationship.
Trump's tariffs targeted China's reliance on U.S. buyers, while U.S. export controls targeted a deeper dependency: the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment Beijing needs to compete at the technological frontier.
Those pressure points remain. But Beijing has developed leverage of its own. China placed seven rare-earth elements under export controls last year, forcing companies to seek government approval to ship them abroad. China accounted for more than 70% of global rare-earth mining and more than 87% of refining and production in 2024, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
In short order, Ford halted Explorer production in Chicago for a week amid magnet shortages, while Japanese and European auto suppliers shut production lines awaiting materials.
Suddenly, the U.S. faced a version of the vulnerability it had spent years trying to create for Beijing: dependence on something the other side could withhold.
"One of China's primary objectives ahead of these meetings is to box the U.S. in diplomatically, to limit the Trump administration's range of action," Hart said, pointing to critical minerals as one tool Beijing has used.
That vulnerability now hangs over Thursday's summit. The current trade truce expires Nov. 10. Rare earths were again on the table in weekend talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Bessent said Wednesday after another meeting with He that the U.S. was "fine with either continuing" the current truce or "examining [a] bigger deal."
Meanwhile, Trump has other cards to play.
U.S. and allied firms control critical parts of the advanced semiconductor ecosystem, and American restrictions limit China's access to its most sophisticated chips and manufacturing equipment. Trump has also allowed limited sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China even as broader restrictions remain in place, making semiconductor access another bargaining point.
That bargaining dynamic is beginning to reach beyond trade.
A $14 billion U.S. arms package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump's approval for months. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the package in abeyance and called it a "very good negotiating chip."
For Beijing, few issues carry higher stakes. China claims Taiwan as its sovereign territory and has never renounced the use of force to achieve unification. Xi also pressed Trump on U.S. arms sales and Taiwan during their May meeting.

articles.title_orig: Trump greets China’s Xi at airport in historic move — as nations agree to trade truce to kick off high-stakes DC visit
articles.title_zh: Trump greets China’s Xi at airport in historic move — as nations agree to trade truce to kick off high-stakes DC visit
articles.content_orig:
Trump greets China’s Xi at airport in historic move — as nations agree to trade truce to kick off high-stakes DC visit
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
WASHINGTON — President Trump personally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US on Wednesday evening — as the nations kicked off a three-day state visit by announcing a trade truce lasting through Jan. 10.
Trump, joined by first lady Melania Trump, made the unusual decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews — a gesture not made by Xi when Trump visited Beijing in May.
The last time an American president greeted a world leader at JBA was in 1962 when John F. Kennedy met British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.
Trump stood at the bottom of the steps to Xi’s plane and shook his hand before escorting him down a red carpet — with a B-1 Lancer bomber making a flyover as the American national anthem played.
Six F-16s and six F-22s were lined up on the tarmac, showcasing US military might.
Trump told reporters as he returned to the White House that it was “a great greeting, and I think they appreciate it — tremendous people.”
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, appeared on Fox News to announce that the US and China agreed not to escalate tariffs until at least 2027.
“We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement,’ the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 — that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said.
“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations.”
Xi’s visit is expected to touch on a wide range of tensions in the US-China relationship, including tariffs, fentanyl exports, artificial intelligence and Beijing’s role in conflicts ranging from Iran to Ukraine.
Trump has repeatedly said he believes a strong personal relationship between the leaders can notch benefits for the American people, though it’s unclear what concrete agreements may come.
Xi will be treated to a state dinner at the White House on Thursday — with the US leader likely to show off his recent renovations, including a new granite helipad with the presidential seal and an enormous ballroom with concrete walls now protruding from the site of the former East Wing.
The relationship between Trump and Xi has had ups and downs, featuring warm in-person greetings but souring during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and during last year’s US-China trade war.
Trump, seeking to force a new trade deal that rebalances the US trade deficit and to punish China’s export of illicit fentanyl, ramped up tariffs on China last year, and Xi retaliated in kind.
The trade clash saw US tariffs on Chinese goods near 150% — before a cooling off following a meeting last October meeting between Trump and Xi in South Korea, where Xi agreed to do more to quash fentanyl exports that killed about 488,000 Americans over the past decade, peaking in 2022 and 2023.
China threatened during the tit-for-tat ramp-up to impose restrictions on rare earth materials, and the US stopped advanced chip sales that Beijing could use to give it a key boost in the artificial intelligence race.
A senior US official told reporters ahead of Xi’s visit that the Trump administration is dissatisfied with Xi’s actions to reduce fentanyl smuggling.
“It does not appear that China has elevated this issue,” the official said. “China is the overwhelming, predominant supplier of precursor chemicals to the cartels in Mexico and remains so. And they have done a number of anecdotal things, including a few arrests recently, but we’d like to see much more systemic change.”
Fentanyl deaths — which Trump cited in his initial wave of tariffs last year — have dipped in the US, but remain elevated and factors such as the availability of test strips and overdose antidotes and improved border detection may have eased the impact. Still, about 35,000 Americans died in the past year.
Trump’s personal warmth with Xi has in the past been coupled with shows of American strength — with the president often recounting a 2017 visit by Xi to Mar-a-Lago. The men were enjoying dessert as Trump revealed that the US had just conducted airstrikes on Syria.
“We had the most beautiful piece of chocolate cake that you’ve ever seen, and President Xi was enjoying it,” Trump remembered afterward. “He was eating his cake. And he was silent.”

The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that's expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump's May visit to China. But it also is a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." A military honor guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present.
