articles.title_orig: Time to prepare is 'now:' Catastrophic floods forecast in Hawaii from Nolo
articles.title_zh: Time to prepare is 'now:' Catastrophic floods forecast in Hawaii from Nolo
articles.content_orig:
Time to prepare is 'now:' Catastrophic floods forecast in Hawaii from Nolo
Newly named Tropical Storm Nolo is raising concern in Hawaii for a "catastrophic" threat from yet another tropical cyclone, for the third time this year.
Heavy rain is forecast to return to the eastern Hawaiian Islands as Nolo formed to the south of the islands, bringing potentially "catastrophic flooding" to areas still recovering from Hurricane Lala flooding.
Nolo is forecast to reach hurricane strength later on Thursday, Sept. 24. A hurricane watch has been issued for the entire Big Island, meaning that hurricane conditions are possible within the watch area.
As of 11 a.m. HT (5 p.m. EDT) on Sept. 23, the center of Nolo was 310 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, and about 500 miles south-southeast of Honolulu. The storm had sustained winds of 40 mph and was moving to the west-northwest at 6 mph.
"The time to prepare for significant heavy rain and flooding impacts on the Big Island is now, as heavy rain becomes more likely by Thursday [Sept. 24] and Friday [Sept. 25]," the hurricane center said in an online bulletin on Sept. 23.
"Periods of heavy rain are likely to continue across the Big Island and Maui through the weekend," according to the hurricane center.
Sharp turn to the north expected
A sharp turn to the north or north-northeast is forecast later on Thursday, Sept. 24, taking the storm near the Big Island of Hawaii on Friday, as a hurricane. Swells are expected to arrive Friday, Sept. 25, spreading west and building over the weekend, creating "life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."
The center of the storm is forecast to be roughly 100 miles south-southeast of the Big Island late Friday night, with sustained winds of 110 mph, just below Category 3 hurricane strength, according to the hurricane center's forecast.
Heavy rain in the forecast
Heavy rain is forecast to start on Wednesday, Sept. 23, and continue through Sept. 26, the hurricane center said. "Life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible from rainfall totals in excess of a foot, especially in areas of steep terrain."
According to AccuWeather, rainfall amounts over three days could reach 24 to 36 inches at higher elevations on the Big Island, with widespread rainfall totals over Hawaii and the eastern side of Maui. But the rainfall rate is expected to have more impact than the total rainfall, the weather service said.
The southeast Big Island "is vulnerable due to ongoing recovery from the flooding during (Hurricane) Lala," said John Bravender, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Honolulu.
Risks for wind and wave impacts are also forecast to increase regardless of the storm's exact track or intensity, and hurricane or tropical storm watches could be issued later today.
"Although it is too soon to specify the exact location and magnitude of impacts, interests in Hawaii should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure that they have their preparedness plan in place," the hurricane center warned.
Flooding forecast for eastern Hawaiian Islands
A flood watch is in effect for the Big Island, Maui, Lanai, Molokai and Kahoolawe from noon Sept. 23 through the afternoon of Saturday, Sept. 26.
Heavy rain on the north side of the intensifying cyclone will develop on Wednesday, Sept. 23, over the Big Island, then spread westward to Maui. The weather service warns of potentially significant flooding, with landslides and possible property damage.
"People should not focus solely on what category this storm becomes," said AccuWeather expert meteorologist Nicholas Arman in an email to USA TODAY. "The greatest danger could be the amount of rain it unloads and how long that rain continues. If the storm slows or stalls close enough to the Big Island, we could be looking at catastrophic flooding and mudslides."
World championship canoe race canceled
Organizers of the annual Na Wahine O Ke Kai, a world championship women’s canoe race scheduled for Sunday, Sept. 27, have canceled the event. The Oahu Hawaiian Canoe Racing Association cited the expected rough conditions offshore. The race from Molokai to Oahu began in 1954 and has been canceled by extreme conditions twice before, in 1980 and 2015.
El Niño a major player this season
Weather troublemaker El Niño – a natural warming of Pacific Ocean water – continues to be a factor in the weather patterns over the Pacific this year. "El Niño is a major reason Hawaii has faced so many tropical threats this season," Arman said. "It promotes warm water and changes wind patterns across the Pacific in ways that can make the central Pacific more favorable for tropical storms and hurricanes to develop and survive. We’ve seen the result this year with storm after storm tracking toward or near the islands."
Hurricane Polo menaces Mexico
Elsewhere in the Pacific, a slightly weakened Hurricane Polo was drifting northward in the Pacific on the morning of Sept. 23, about 165 miles south of Zihuatanejo, Mexico, with peak sustained winds of 150 mph. Tropical storm watches and warnings are in effect along the country’s southern coast.
The hurricane is forecast to begin moving westward by Sept. 24, then turn northward by Sept. 26 and approach the Southern California Baja Peninsula. The official forecast calls for the center of the hurricane to be roughly 200 miles west of Cabo San Lucas on the morning of Sunday, Sept. 27, as a hurricane, with peak sustained winds of 105 mph.
Hurricane Polo becomes a record breaker
Polo rapidly intensified earlier in the week, becoming a Category 5 hurricane with 180 mph winds, increasing its wind speeds by 95 mph in less than 24 hours.
"The hurricane tore through records, strengthening from a disorganized tropical depression to a Category 5 hurricane in a remarkable 42 hours, the fastest of any system on record in the western hemisphere," said Michael Lowry, a hurricane specialist with WPLG-TV in Miami. A low-pressure reading in the hurricane's eye on Sept. 22 made it the second most intense eastern Pacific hurricane ever recorded, Lowry said. The most intense was 2015's Hurricane Patricia.
Odalys spins in the open Pacific
Hurricane Odalys has also joined the Pacific storm party this week.
As of 2 a.m. PT, the center of Odalys was about 1,295 miles south-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California Peninsula. It had maximum sustained winds of 75 mph, the hurricane center said.
It poses no threat to any land areas.
Odalys is forecast to hit peak intensity on the evening of Sept. 24, then weaken. The potential still exists for Odalys, as a tropical storm, to have some interaction with Hurricane Polo, the hurricane center said in a forecast discussion. The centers of the two storms are forecast to be roughly 600 miles apart on the morning of Sept. 27.
Atlantic remains hurricane-free
In the Atlantic basin, a low-pressure system redeveloped into Tropical Depression Fay, the hurricane center said Wednesday.
Some strengthening is possible during the next couple of days, but gradual weakening should occur thereafter, the NHC said.
In addition to Fay, forecasters are watching an area of disturbed weather near Africa for possible development into another tropical depression, the hurricane center said.
However, due to strong upper-level winds that will act to shear off the tops of the storms, neither storm is forecast to reach hurricane strength, which will continue the trend that's prevented hurricanes from forming in the Atlantic this season.
Polo pushes monsoonal rains into New Mexico
A strong band of monsoonal moisture pushing ahead of Hurricane Polo is soaking much of New Mexico.
Overnight on Sept. 22, heavy rain sent the Rio Hondo River up more than six feet before it crested, according to the weather service office in Albuquerque. The rain is expected to continue, contributing to the risk of flash flooding through Thursday, particularly in eastern New Mexico.

articles.title_orig: UK PM Burnham wants 'outdated' football drinking ban scrapped
articles.title_zh: UK PM Burnham wants 'outdated' football drinking ban scrapped
articles.content_orig:
Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".
The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.
Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.
The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".
The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.
Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.
Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.
Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.
Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.
"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.
"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."
Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.
The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.
A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.
A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games".
He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour.
"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games."
He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area".
FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league".
He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed."
A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined.
The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials.
The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games.

articles.title_orig: As Xi Visits Washington, Trump Plays Down China’s Actions Against U.S. Interests
articles.title_zh: As Xi Visits Washington, Trump Plays Down China’s Actions Against U.S. Interests
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has spent years trying to squeeze China — imposing tariffs, cutting off access to advanced technology and pressing U.S. allies to reduce their dependence on Beijing. When he begins meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, he'll juxtapose the long-standing bluster with the pomp and circumstance the leaders lavish on each other.
The pageantry began immediately. Upon arrival at Maryland's Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening, Xi and Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan were greeted by Trump, First Lady Melania Trump and a swarm of U.S. service members, some of whom rolled out a large red carpet for the visiting leader.
Before leaving the tarmac, Xi was treated to a flyover during a rendition of the U.S. national anthem.
The two-day tête-à-tête will take place as Trump confronts a China that has proved harder to isolate and allies increasingly reluctant to line up behind the U.S. to do it.
Part of that is Beijing's doing. China has deepened trade ties around the world while building leverage of its own, most notably through rare earths. Its global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year, reaching a record $1.2 trillion for 2025 even as its exports to the U.S. dropped.
But the shift also reflects Trump's approach. Since returning to office, fights over tariffs, defense spending and personal spats have strained relationships with traditional allies even as Trump has pursued a more transactional relationship with Xi.
Countries Washington has traditionally counted on to magnify its power are increasingly seeking room to maneuver between the world's two largest economies.
As a result, Trump enters Thursday's summit facing a test of whether strains with U.S. allies have made it harder to marshal American power against Xi.
"China is presenting itself to the world as the stable counterweight to an erratic and violent United States," said Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution think tank. "America retains unmatched power on the world stage, but leverage requires a united front and there are a shrinking number of countries willing to follow America's lead right now."
For decades, one of the U.S.'s biggest advantages over China has been its network of allies and partners. When the U.S. restricted technology or imposed sanctions, bringing major economies in Europe and Asia along made those measures harder for Beijing to evade.
China still lacks anything comparable: The Lowy Institute, an independent Australian foreign-policy think tank, scored the U.S. defense networks at 81.4 on a scale of 100, versus 18.9 for China in 2025. But Beijing does not need U.S. allies to switch sides to erode that advantage. It only needs them to become less willing to move with Washington, Hass and other China experts said.
"When democratic countries don't have public support for a counterpart, it raises the cost for leaders to align with the United States," Hass told CNBC. "It lowers the cost for leaders to defy the United States."
Trump has taken a sledgehammer to relationships with allies. He's clashed with NATO over defense spending, threatened to reduce the U.S. troop presence in much of Europe while announcing plans Tuesday to add troops in Greenland after threatening to take over the island and imposed tariffs on the U.S.'s northern neighbor Canada.
"Although our biggest economic complaints regarding China's economy are shared by many of our allies and partners, the current U.S. approach is to attack all of those countries ... instead of forming a common front," said Melanie Hart, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
Meanwhile, public confidence in the U.S. as a reliable partner has fallen. In Canada, the share of people who described the U.S. as a reliable partner fell from 83% in 2022 to 35% this year, according to Pew Research Center in June. In Germany, the share who said Washington considers other countries' interests when making foreign policy fell from 60% in 2023 to 23%.
Canada this month was invited to be the first "associate member" of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government seeks deeper defense ties with Europe and less reliance on the U.S.
Foreign allies "worry that as soon as they make a deal with us, Washington will undercut them in some way that they will then regret," Hart told CNBC.
China has sought to capitalize on that opening, not necessarily by persuading countries to choose Beijing over Washington, but by making the choice less binary.
The country remains a U.S. security partner and a strategic competitor of China, with troops from both countries still deployed along their disputed Himalayan border. Yet Xi visited India this month for the first time in seven years as the two countries took what Tanvi Madan, a senior fellow at Brookings, called "baby steps" toward stabilizing relations.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese data, and Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to strengthen business and transport links despite unresolved security disputes.
"Uncertainty over Trump's approach to Beijing and strains in India's own relationship with the U.S. have given India another reason to keep relations with China on steadier ground," Madan told CNBC. "Even a tactical détente between the U.S., India and China can have downstream impacts on India's strategic environment."
The changing balance of leverage is most tangible in the economic relationship.
Trump's tariffs targeted China's reliance on U.S. buyers, while U.S. export controls targeted a deeper dependency: the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment Beijing needs to compete at the technological frontier.
Those pressure points remain. But Beijing has developed leverage of its own. China placed seven rare-earth elements under export controls last year, forcing companies to seek government approval to ship them abroad. China accounted for more than 70% of global rare-earth mining and more than 87% of refining and production in 2024, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
In short order, Ford halted Explorer production in Chicago for a week amid magnet shortages, while Japanese and European auto suppliers shut production lines awaiting materials.
Suddenly, the U.S. faced a version of the vulnerability it had spent years trying to create for Beijing: dependence on something the other side could withhold.
"One of China's primary objectives ahead of these meetings is to box the U.S. in diplomatically, to limit the Trump administration's range of action," Hart said, pointing to critical minerals as one tool Beijing has used.
That vulnerability now hangs over Thursday's summit. The current trade truce expires Nov. 10. Rare earths were again on the table in weekend talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Bessent said Wednesday after another meeting with He that the U.S. was "fine with either continuing" the current truce or "examining [a] bigger deal."
Meanwhile, Trump has other cards to play.
U.S. and allied firms control critical parts of the advanced semiconductor ecosystem, and American restrictions limit China's access to its most sophisticated chips and manufacturing equipment. Trump has also allowed limited sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China even as broader restrictions remain in place, making semiconductor access another bargaining point.
That bargaining dynamic is beginning to reach beyond trade.
A $14 billion U.S. arms package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump's approval for months. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the package in abeyance and called it a "very good negotiating chip."
For Beijing, few issues carry higher stakes. China claims Taiwan as its sovereign territory and has never renounced the use of force to achieve unification. Xi also pressed Trump on U.S. arms sales and Taiwan during their May meeting.

articles.title_orig: Trump officials weigh rolling back beef import plan as GOP midterm panic spreads
articles.title_zh: Trump officials weigh rolling back beef import plan as GOP midterm panic spreads
articles.content_orig:
Former Ag Sec. Criticizes Beef Imports
Johanns: Beef Imports Send Wrong Message, Hurting Ranchers Just as Profits Return
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (DTN) -- Mike Johanns, a former Republican Agriculture secretary, said Monday the Trump administration's move to increase beef imports is hurting cattle producers who had finally begun recovering after years of weak returns.
Johanns, a former Nebraska governor and U.S. senator who served as agriculture secretary under President George W. Bush, spoke at the start of an Ag Outlook Forum in downtown Kansas City.
Without directly mentioning President Donald Trump, Johanns criticized the federal government's intervention into beef markets. He described the issue as "white hot" in cattle country. Now that ranchers are benefiting from the stronger side of the cattle cycle, Johanns said the federal government should not intervene simply because beef prices are high.
"If you would take the last 20 years in the cattle industry, 10 of those years I lost money, maybe 12," Johanns said. "A handful of those years were probably break-even at best."
He added, "Finally, they're making some money, and the government steps in, and I just don't agree with that."
Citing high beef prices, Trump last month announced plans to allow 300,000 metric tons (661.4 million pounds) of imported lean beef to enter the country tariff-free over three months. The resulting ground beef would then be sold at a discounted price. Major farm groups immediately called for Trump to reverse course on the plan, but there has been no official word on changes. Responding to industry criticism, USDA rolled out new plans to promote heifer retention, expand local processing and strengthen U.S.-origin beef labels.
Johanns estimated the resulting decline in cattle values cost the average producer somewhere between $250 and $500 per head.
Returns have improved over the past couple of years, particularly for ranchers and cow-calf operators, Johanns said. That optimism was shaken by the administration's announcement that it would increase beef imports in an effort to lower beef prices for consumers.

"Finally, they're kind of healing the pain and seeing some opportunity going forward," he said. "Maybe we can expand the ranch. Maybe we can expand the herd. Then all of a sudden, there's this announcement out of Washington, and they're going, 'Whoa, wait a second! Where did that come from?'"
Producers who previously lacked the cash to make improvements were beginning to do so, he said. Others could consider buying a neighboring ranch if it became available. Johanns said those stronger returns reflected the traditional cattle cycle after years when ranchers frequently struggled to make money.
"Who steps up and says, 'Well, I think they're making too much money?' Our government," Johanns said.
He said producers were largely left to absorb the losses when cattle markets were weak.
"I hated it when the ranchers were losing money, but most of the time, they were," Johanns said. "They just had friendly bankers. That's the only way they could survive."
Ranchers' reaction goes beyond frustration over a short-term decline in cattle prices, the former secretary said. Stronger cattle prices had reached the point where producers repair their finances and consider investments that had been difficult to make during leaner years.
Johanns also questioned whether increasing imported beef would save consumers enough money to justify the financial impact on cattle producers. He said it would only have a modest impact, "maybe a few cents or something on a hamburger," but added that the detriment to cattle producers outweighs the consumer benefit.
The former secretary also touched on his own decisions to oversee beef imports and exports during his time at USDA. One of his biggest challenges when he became Agriculture secretary in 2005 was reopening foreign markets that had closed to U.S. beef following the discovery of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE, in Washington state in late 2003.
Johanns said that as he pressed countries such as Japan to reopen their markets to U.S. beef, foreign officials challenged the United States over restrictions it had placed on cattle and beef from other countries, including Canada.
"If you want others to buy our beef, what's your policy going to be on the other end of it?" Johanns said.
Reopening the U.S. market to Canadian cattle was controversial at the time, he noted, with cattlemen's organizations divided over the move. Johanns, however, drew a distinction between imports needed as part of a reciprocal trading system and importing more beef specifically to drive down domestic prices.
"To bring in beef to discount it -- like there's something wrong with our beef here -- that's not set well," Johanns said. "I don't think this is a giant revelation for anybody anywhere in the ag industry, but it is the reality of what's going on out there. There's just some really hard feelings."

articles.title_orig: US senators press for quick Chinese vehicle ban this week as Xi visits
articles.title_zh: US senators press for quick Chinese vehicle ban this week as Xi visits
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — As President Donald Trump meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, U.S. politicians as well as the global automotive industry are warning that allowing Chinese automakers to enter the market could be a Pandora's box.
Trump earlier this month said he might be "OK" letting Chinese automakers into the U.S. if they produced vehicles domestically, leading a consortium of auto trade groups representing every major facet of the American auto industry to urge him to rethink that position.
It was an uncharacteristically unified message from automakers operating in the U.S., franchised dealers and suppliers. More than two dozen Democratic lawmakers followed that push with their own letter, urging Trump to keep in place U.S. restrictions against Chinese automakers.
"It's not at this point a partisan issue," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., told reporters Wednesday. "It's about whether we want to make cars in America and whether we want a manufacturing base that can pivot when we need it. If we want that, we shouldn't let them in our country."
Trump is scheduled to host Xi and a delegation from China on Thursday and Friday that reportedly could include Wang Chuanfu, founder of BYD, China's largest automaker, and Robin Zeng, founder of CATL, the world's top battery maker for electric vehicles.
Michael Dunne, an expert on China's automotive industry and a former General Motors executive, said even the potential that those two executives could attend underscores the importance of Xi's trip for the U.S. auto industry.
GM CEO Mary Barra is also expected to be among the attendees at Trump's state dinner for Xi, Reuters reported Wednesday, along with several other U.S. executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
As for America's other largest automakers, Ford Motor declined to disclose whether CEO Jim Farley will be attending after the Department of Transportation criticized the company for its Chinese ties, including a licensing deal with CATL. Reuters reported Chrysler parent Stellantis said CEO Antonio Filosa is out of the country and not planning to attend.
Industry insiders and onlookers have expressed concerns similar to those raised by automakers and lawmakers as bipartisan bills to ban Chinese automakers from the U.S. move through Congress.
The pressure campaign comes as Chinese automakers have been rapidly expanding outside of their domestic market, especially to Europe and Central and South America. There's fear among global automakers that Chinese rivals, like BYD and Geely, which are heavily subsidized by their governments, could flood global markets, undercutting domestic production and vehicle prices.
Dunne said he doesn't believe those concerns are overblown. He said Chinese automakers would "quickly overwhelm America's auto industry, just as it is now ravaging Europe."
Global market share for Chinese brands jumped nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. The automakers' market share in Europe was virtually nothing in 2020 but hit 12% in August, according to Germany-based Dataforce.
"China's scores of automakers are currently engaged in a fight-to-the-death price war at home," Dunne wrote in a post Monday. "There's red ink everywhere. Access to the U.S., by far the most lucrative car market in the world, is like a giant tank of life-saving oxygen."
'Attacking very aggressively'
For much of this century, China was one of the largest and fastest-growing markets in the world. Non-China automakers flocked to the historically enclosed country with hopes of massive sales and profits.
But after years of success for automakers such as GM, the Chinese automotive sector has rapidly changed from an insular industry to the biggest exporter of vehicles globally.
China's growth has been fueled by government funding for companies as well as a culture of innovation and speed the country has instilled in its workers, experts said. The decision to ramp up exports has come on the heels of a slowing Chinese market and plant underutilization.
Christian Meunier, Nissan Motor chairman of the Americas, described competing against Chinese automakers as a "hell of a challenge" in countries outside of the U.S.
"They have decent product but it's all dumping," he told CNBC during a recent interview. "We know we're not competing with [automakers], we're competing against the governments. … They're attacking very aggressively."
Meunier said the Japanese automaker has been trying to battle the Chinese as best as it can through growing scale globally to lower costs and become more efficient.
"We need to get ready for the day when they come to the U.S. because it will happen one day. Hopefully not tomorrow, but it will happen one day," he said.
Dunne said China's ambitions and ways of doing business are vastly different from those of U.S. allies, which makes it different from allowing imports from Japan, South Korea and other countries.
"As Xi Jinping has alluded to many times, the goal for China is to 'make other countries more dependent on China and China less dependent on other countries.' That's not a friendly posture," Dunne said.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Mississippi police make 2nd arrest in death of Black woman found hanging from tree, seek 3rd suspect
articles.title_zh: Mississippi police make 2nd arrest in death of Black woman found hanging from tree, seek 3rd suspect
articles.content_orig:
Police make 2nd arrest in death of Tasia Fortune, Mississippi woman found hanging from tree
Police in Mississippi have arrested a second man in the death of a Black woman found hanging from a tree and have issued an arrest warrant for a third suspect.
Jackson police said late Tuesday that they arrested 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd Jr. in the death of 29-year-old Tasia Fortune, whose body was found hanging behind an abandoned home in the city on Aug. 3.
Like Fortune and the first man arrested, 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, Lloyd is Black. He appeared at a brief hearing Wednesday in Jackson.
Fortune's mother Christy Spivey, who attended the hearing, said afterward that she was ecstatic to see arrests made in her daughter's death. She said that neither she nor several of her daughter's friends knew Lloyd, and she cautioned that everyone is innocent until proven guilty.
"My family is not the only family that this is affecting," Spivey said of the defendants' families. "I feel for them as well. The only difference is that mine can never come back."
"I'll never truly have peace," she said.
Ratliff was arrested in September on murder charges. He pleaded not guilty and remains jailed without bond.
After Ratliff's arrest, Jackson's police chief, RaShall Brackney, said Ratliff had an "association" with Fortune, but she didn't elaborate.
Police said in a statement that they issued an arrest warrant for a third suspect, but gave no details about that person's identity or alleged link to Fortune's death. They also said they expect to issue additional warrants. After Ratliff's arrest, Brackney said police interviewed over a dozen people and collected forensic evidence as part of the investigation.
Although police haven't suggested a possible motive for the killing or said whether they think race played a role, the case has attracted widespread attention because the manner of death recalled lynchings in the Southern state. Her death also comes one year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused White man, in Vicksburg, Mississippi. Both deaths were ruled suicides, though Reed's family and attorneys have called for an independent autopsy.
A Kentucky native, Fortune had four children and had been living in Jackson for about a decade, relatives said. Spivey said earlier this month that the Fortune's loved ones "still don't have a lot of answers."
Spivey previously said her daughter struggled with homelessness in recent years, and that she wasn't sure where her daughter was living at the time of her death. She said that before her death, her daughter had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order.

articles.title_orig: Sean Payton: All good with Mike Macdonald, incident helped us handle training camp videos
articles.title_zh: Sean Payton: All good with Mike Macdonald, incident helped us handle training camp videos
articles.content_orig:
Broncos head coach Sean Payton got his chance to address Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald’s comments about a 2024 disagreement between the teams at his Wednesday press conference.
Macdonald said earlier in the day that he called Payton to apologize after comments he intended to be off the record about Payton getting upset about the Seahawks’ use of fan videos from training camp to prepare for a 2024 game went public. Payton said he and Macdonald are good and said he called Seahawks General Manager John Schneider “shooting before I started looking” because he didn’t know how the Seahawks had obtained the videos.
The videos were posted on social media and Payton said that the incident wound up in a positive way because it allowed the Broncos to address videotaping of their practices.
“Talking with them, it allowed us to figure out how to handle our training camp relative to videos,” Payton said. “I don’t think anything was intentional by fans. We did some research online of what was available and that’s kind of how we changed our policy.”
Payton called the entire episode “eye-opening” in terms of how information from open practices can circulate and both sides will likely be sticking to official game tape to prepare for their Week 6 game.

articles.title_orig: China silent as US touts plan for AI safety alerts that omits tech experts
articles.title_zh: China silent as US touts plan for AI safety alerts that omits tech experts
articles.content_orig:
This week, the US and China, the two world leaders on AI, finally started talks meant to keep the whole world safe from emerging safety risks. But whether meetings between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping can lead to a reliable global governance framework for AI depends on how much the fierce rivals are actually willing to cooperate.
It’s clear Trump wants it to seem like discussions are going well. Before Trump and Xi meet on Thursday and Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that both sides had already discussed setting up a new AI safety notification mechanism. If China agrees to participate, that would create an open line for either side to send alerts when their country’s AI systems pose threats or behave unpredictably. The same channel, Bessent said, could allow the countries to share their “vision of common goals.”
However, the proposal comes at a time when China may not be ready to trust the US to have AI safety conversations that aren’t about limiting China’s capabilities. Not only has Trump steadily increased export controls that explicitly seek to block China from accessing technology to advance AI, but Congress is mulling bills that would cut the country off from more chips and hardware. Adding to tensions, just two weeks ago, Trump’s Justice Department accused six of China’s leading AI makers of stealing from US frontier labs, which China has strongly disputed.
Some US-China experts told Ars that there were concerns that China might cancel talks, but China seemingly isn’t taking offense to Trump’s rhetoric. Even Truth Social posts where Trump insists that America must dominate China on AI—declaring “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so”—didn’t keep China from showing up.
Notably, China has yet to publicly acknowledge the proposed alert system. Even if China bought into the system, people familiar with Bessent’s plan told Politico that the plan to monitor safety alerts appears superficial, since it involves no officials with technical expertise who could be trusted to assess the urgency of risks described in communications.
Describing the significance of the arrangement, one source mocked the plan, saying “the scientific, technical term is BS.”
Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at a Georgetown University think tank called the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, monitors national security applications of AI and US-China tech competition. He agreed it’s a red flag that there’s no tech body of tech experts monitoring the channel.
“It’s an existing channel, which I think is better than creating a whole new channel,” Bresnick told Ars. But if both sides had tech experts, the US and China could have really high-level conversations about how they’re assessing risk. That’s particularly important when discussing military risks, Bresnick emphasized.
“I think it’s better than nothing for sure, but I don’t have a lot of confidence that that is going to make a major difference going forward,” Bresnick said.
Low expectations for Trump talks
Su Lian Jye, a chief analyst at a global technology research and advisory group called Omdia, told the South China Morning Post that the AI alerts may help “promote more transparency,” but it won’t make either side less wary of the other.
“I don’t think the dialog will remove all concerns and differences on distillation, pricing competition, and pacing,” Su said.
Praising the plan as a good start to open dialogues, Su suggested that much more cooperation would be needed to make the safety mechanism meaningful.
“Turning the proposal into an effective tool would require both countries to agree on risk classifications, notification triggers, response protocols, and regular review procedures,” he said.
Perhaps that will come up when Trump and Xi meet later this week, with AI supposedly at the top of the agenda.
It’s unclear what will be discussed, but critics concerned about the most urgent AI safety risks fear that Bessent’s announcement indicates that Trump has modest ambitions for the summit.
On CBS’s “Face the Nation,” US Representative Ro Khanna—the ranking Democrat on the US House Select Committee on Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party—suggested that talks between Trump and Xi should go much further than setting up a line between two officials with no tech expertise.
He argued Trump should be asking Xi for an international agreement that urgently includes “banning any recursive self-improving AI” and “safeguards so that AI can’t be misused by people for biological nuclear weapons.”
China suspicious of AI safety talks
Many experts described sharing safety alerts as a decent first step in improving US-China coordination on AI, which Trump’s incoming “AI czar” could then possibly build on.
Alvin Wang Graylin, a global technology strategist and digital fellow at Stanford Digital Economy Lab, has spent decades weighing geopolitical risks. Most recently, he’s advised governments and tech leaders on AI policy and global governance, including sharing recommendations on how to set up a notification system like the one Bessent proposed.
Graylin told Ars that he was surprised to see that such a “positive” development had already come out of this week’s talks with China. And it seemed encouraging that both countries already have another meeting scheduled in November.
“What that shows is that both sides are seeing value in the discussion,” Graylin said. “Otherwise, there would not be a follow-on.”
Graylin suggested the US and China share many AI risks. Not just the supposedly existential risk that AI leaders started recently claiming required a slowdown, but also risks from bad actors like hackers or terrorists wielding AI to attack either country’s infrastructure.
There’s much that the US and China can learn from each other if they talk seriously. Graylin said that China regularly audits AI models and could share knowledge from hundreds of audits, since the US has only just begun auditing AI. What China could gain from the US is perhaps more experience auditing frontier models.
“I think both sides are going to come to the realization” that controlling AI risk will “require cooperation,” Graylin said.
Bresnick suggested that ongoing talks could be an opportunity to “explore how each side views risks.” While the US has been combating public fears of uncontrollable AI, in China, “there’s just not the same fear right now about AI,” Bresnick said, largely because the state feels that it can control AI.
That may change as China’s advanced AI catches up to the US, Bresnick said. He expects that US-China discussions could ramp up in the next six months to a year, as China starts to see the same level of emerging capabilities.
However, for now, the very different way that China views risk may deter America’s biggest rival from coming to the table to talk about risks from terrorists or hackers, Bresnick said. Especially if the US continues tying the AI safety discussion to keeping America ahead.
When Trump or CEOs like Sam Altman advocate for American-led global AI standards, all China probably sees is the US wielding safety discussions as a way to lock in its advantage, he said. Those concerns may even render Bessent’s alert system useless in the long term if China feels that “AI safety” is a code word for suppressing Chinese AI.
“I think there are reasons [for China] to view this notification mechanism with suspicion,” Bresnick said.
Trump’s “deeply flawed” AI race
Graylin has warned that the US is too caught up in pushing a “deeply flawed” narrative about “winning” an “AI race” that most likely will benefit no one.
In reality, there are at least two races, one for intelligence and one for market dominance. Currently the US is making more money on frontier AI but is falling behind in the race for users globally. articles.title_orig: Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
articles.title_zh: Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
articles.content_orig:
Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
Clavicular, the controversial streamer who rose from the corners of the internet to the mainstream advocating for extreme tactics to achieve physical attractiveness, now finds his internet fame spilling into the courtroom.
Braden Peters, better known for his online moniker, has been charged in Massachusetts court with rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to an underage person, court records show.
Peters, 20, has become the visible face of the "looksmaxxing" movement. He’s gone to extremes such as hitting himself in the face with a hammer so his bones supposedly grow back sharper and taking small amounts of methamphetamine in an attempt to suppress his appetite. Offshoots of the trend, which are associated with the "manosphere," have ventured into sexist, misogynistic and racist philosophies, while Peters himself has drawn criticism for using racial slurs during his streams.
The viral nature of his controversial soundbites and short-form content helped usher what was once a niche subculture on obscure Reddit forums into the mainstream on TikTok, Instagram and Kik, where he’s collectively amassed more than 2.7 million followers. Now, the turn in his trajectory offers a window into the pitfalls of a movement drawing young men online in droves.
What is 'looksmaxxing,' the 'manosphere?'
"Looksmaxxing" is the process of maximizing one’s physical appearance through hygiene, fitness and style.
The term has gone mainstream and can have positive implications, such as getting healthy or working out more in the hopes of finding more confidence in the dating world.
However, the looksmaxxing movement has roots in online incel culture, which villainizes women, and has become a new subset of the "manosphere," a digital collection of websites, videos and social media that promote male supremacy and advocate for traditional gender roles.
How young men get sucked into 'looksmaxxing'
The combination of technology and the natural insecurities that arise during teenage years creates a "perfect storm" for innocuous sports and health spaces to tune young men into radical content, Gary Barker, the president of Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, an organization that advocates for healthy manhood, previously told USA TODAY.
"They’re going there with kind of innocent intentions, but without somebody else supporting them, that innocent intention can become a follower who drops their critical thinking," Barker said.
Looksmaxxing creators have become a modern extension for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Among these creators, such as Kareem Shami, an early adopter who encourages "mewing," and Alex Costa, who focuses on "softmaxxing" with style and haircare, Clavicular has become the most extreme, advocating for surgical upgrades. In June, he livestreamed his rhinoplasty on Kick, undergoing four procedures ahead of Paris Fashion Week in what he called "Ascension Week."
As his looksmaxxing tactics have been more extreme, so have his far-right, sexist and racist rhetoric.
His streams often feature degrading language regarding women, and he was seen partying in Miami with Andrew and Tristan Tate, manosphere creator Sneako and far-right nationalist Nick Fuentes in January, where the group was filmed singing along to Ye’s "Heil Hitler."
On Sept. 4, Romanian prosecutors indicted 39-year-old Andrew Tate for allegedly trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering, and his 38-year-old brother Tristan Tate for alleged complicity.
"The current version of the manosphere has become much more mainstream than it used to be," said University of Wisconsin-Madison public affairs professor Mariel Barnes, whose research focuses on backlash to gender equality and the manosphere. "You don't need to hide who you are anymore if you're a raging misogynist."
Extreme fringes of the manosphere have orchestrated or praised violent attacks against women, a trend Netflix’s 2025 crime drama "Adolescence" highlighted by following the story of a 13-year-old boy who was radicalized by misogynistic culture online.
Peters' September charges come after his teen protege Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza sued him in April for physical and sexual abuse after an incident at his Cape Cod, Massachusetts, home in May 2025. Mendoza alleged that the content creator had sex with her while she was intoxicated and without consent, and injected her with an "unapproved drug" during a livestream when she was 16.
Young men who tune into extreme content and are isolated from women and other men are more likely to take on radical views or engage in violence, according to Barnes.
"If you are constantly consuming this content and you are isolated and women are responsible for the bad things that are happening to you, it's very dehumanizing, right?" Barnes said. "You don't see women as humans anymore, or as peers or as friends, and that dehumanization gives you permission to treat them as less than human."

articles.title_orig: Judge appears skeptical of Trump’s effort to ban news outlets from White House
articles.title_zh: Judge appears skeptical of Trump’s effort to ban news outlets from White House
articles.content_orig:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.
Trump is bracing to lose his latest fight with the press
Trump’s lawyers said he barred three news outlets from the White House on security grounds. A judge seemed skeptical.
A hearing on President Donald Trump’s White House press ban ended without a ruling this afternoon — an admittedly anticlimactic outcome, but one that will likely change very soon.
The Trump-appointed judge in the case, Timothy Kelly, appeared skeptical of the administration’s arguments for banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds last week. Kelly said he would rule “as soon as possible.” Until then, the ban remains in place.
By all accounts, Trump’s case is a feeble one. While the Justice Department attempted to argue on Wednesday that the three outlets’ reporting jeopardized national security, Trump himself kind of gave the game away last week when he said he had singled these organizations out over what he characterized as negative and inaccurate stories.
The move sat poorly even with people and institutions you’d expect to be sympathetic to Trump: Fox News was one of several outlets that boycotted White House events this week to protest the ban, for instance.
And ahead of today’s hearing, Trump himself seemed primed to lose. In a Truth Social post on Monday, he promised he would “almost without question” appeal any decision against him.
This is all emblematic of how Trump has escalated his attacks on the news media in his second term: not just by insulting and demeaning the press, but also by weaponizing otherwise neutral-seeming rules.
Every administration has policies that regulate who can access the White House grounds and under what conditions, for instance. But in early 2025, the White House took control of the press pool — the rotating group of reporters that frequently travels with the president — and soon sought to exclude disfavored organizations.
More insidiously, Trump has mobilized regulatory agencies like the Federal Communications Commission against his perceived critics, in some cases even threatening to revoke the licenses of local TV stations that air coverage and commentary he disagrees with.
While no licenses have actually been suspended, the FCC has mysteriously pulled some up for unscheduled review. And just the prospect of government retaliation has been enough to force some content off the air: Just two weeks ago, the late-night comedy host Jimmy Kimmel said his show wouldn’t air a scheduled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico because of the FCC’s new scrutiny of political content.
This playbook isn’t a Trump original, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp has explained. In fact, weaponizing broadcast regulations was also a favored technique of former Hungarian Prime Minister (and infamous strongman) Viktor Orbán, who successfully used licensing rules and other bureaucratic technicalities to force independent media outlets into submission.
Likewise, revoking the press credentials of critical reporters has long been a favorite tactic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Nico Perrino, the executive vice president of the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a briefing on Wednesday: “These are things that are done by regimes that we do not want to emulate.”
Lest these comparisons get you down, however, recall that neither Hungary nor Russia has all the defenses that the US does. Defenses like, for example, an independent court system.
➨ Date a little differently. It’s not just your imagination: The search for love has become weirdly intolerant and antagonistic. One new survey finds that the percentage of singles with a must-have trait list they’re checking off has risen to a whopping 34 percent. Experts blame larger cultural changes, the rise of dating apps, and negative social media narratives. But you can fight back in your own dating life by letting your guard (and maybe your standards!) down a little bit.

articles.title_orig: Questions remain over China’s $17 billion U.S. ag purchase commitment
articles.title_zh: Questions remain over China’s $17 billion U.S. ag purchase commitment
articles.content_orig:
Questions remain over China’s $17 billion U.S. ag purchase commitment
Questions remain about China’s ag purchase commitments as the U.S. and China meet tomorrow.
“You never know in these high level discussions what you’ll walk out with.” says Justin Benavidez, the chief economist at the USDA.
Benavidez says China has been making progress on its 25 million metric ton soybean commitment, but what’s happening with the $17 billion in extra ag product purchases is unclear.
He says China’s relisting of U.S. beef plants for export is a positive development for trade barriers.
“Now, they’ve obviously put in place some tariff rate quota thresholds that are pretty aggressive and might, in turn, keep us out of the marketplace, to some extent, for beef exports. But I think the relisting of the plants was a positive, overall, story for beef.”
Seth Meyer with the University of Missouri’s Food and Ag Policy Research Institute says there’s still uncertainty about what products will make up those additional purchases.
“Is it other meats, is it ethanol, what counts under this, and how close will we get to that?” asks Meyer.
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet on Thursday.
Benavidez and Meyer were part of the Ag Outlook Forum, sponsored by the Ag Business Council of Kansas City and Agri-Pulse, in Kansas City, Missouri this week.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.title_zh: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).
Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.
Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.
That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).
Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.
Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.
I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.
Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.

articles.title_orig: Treasury yields surge to near 20-year high as oil jumps back above $103 per barrel
articles.title_zh: Treasury yields surge to near 20-year high as oil jumps back above $103 per barrel
articles.content_orig:
The yields on U.S. Treasury bonds jumped Wednesday and oil prices rose, sending stocks tumbling as investors braced for the prospect of future Fed rate hikes.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, especially mortgages, rose as high as 5.13%, its highest level since 2007. Indeed, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.26% on Wednesday, according to Mortgage News Daily. That’s the highest point since Jan. 13, 2025 — and of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The 10-year yield’s rise was its sharpest one-day jump since April 9, 2025, a week after Trump’s tariffs began roiling global markets, according to Dow Jones data.
Yields on 5- and 30-year Treasury bonds also hit levels that had not seen since before the 2008 global financial crisis.
Stocks fell in response to the rise in yields and oil prices. The Nasdaq Composite index ended the trading session down 1.13%, and the S&P 500 fell 0.75%. The Dow declined 352 points.
International Brent crude oil climbed 3.8% to end the day at $103.08 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil closed up 1.8% at $92.16. The rise in oil prices snapped a streak of five days of declines.
Rising oil prices often translate into higher bond yields due to the effect that higher energy costs can have on inflation more broadly.
One of the primary drivers of Wednesday’s rise in bond yields was the release of new economic data that revealed rising inflation.
Yields rise sharply when Treasury bonds sell off.
“US business activity growth accelerated for a fourth successive month in September to reach the fastest rate for over five years,” S&P Global reported in its latest purchasing managers index reading .
“Firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices seen during the month, which will add further to the upward pressure on selling prices and inflation in the coming months,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Investors viewed the data as likely to increase the odds of multiple Federal Reserve interest rate hikes later this year and next. As of late Wednesday afternoon, market odds for a Fed rate hike in October were up to more 70%.
One Fed policymaker signaled that would likely vote in favor of another rate increase during the Fed’s Oct. 27-28 meeting.
“Risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded,” Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr told a housing conference in Chicago.
“In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion,” he said.
Crude oil trading desks Wednesday were focused on the latest developments in the Iran war.
A day earlier, the price of oil had fallen sharply after Trump said U.S. officials were holding talks with Iranian representatives at the U.N. General Assembly. But hopes that the talks would produce tangible results were dashed by a new report Wednesday that a cargo vessel had been “stuck by an unknown projectile” in the Strait of Hormuz.
Lying just off Iran’s southwestern coast, the critical chokepoint for global energy supplies has been under a military blockade for seven months.
Trump further shook energy markets Tuesday when he said he supported a ban on U.S. exports of diesel fuel.
“Let’s not send out the diesel,” Trump said to reporters at the U.N. “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.”
Trump’s remarks sent European benchmark diesel futures higher by as much 7% early Wednesday.
But experts and energy industry groups warn that a ban on diesel exports would spell even higher gas prices for Americans.
“Removing U.S. diesel from the market could instead result in reduced refinery runs, global economic damage and even higher U.S. prices,” the American Petroleum Institute said in a statement.
Trump’s Energy Secretary Chris Wright also said a ban would not help to bring down prices.
“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” he said Wednesday at an event in New York, according to Reuters .
Wright added at an event hosted by The New York Times later Wednesday that “nobody wants a full blanket ban or zero exports of diesel.”
“That’s not being discussed,” he said.
Inflation-sensitive stocks, such as travel companies and large technology firms, were the hardest hit by Wednesday’s reversal.
The S&P’s biggest sector loser was utilities, which contains many of the companies leading the AI data center boom. Higher interest rates could potentially add billions of dollars to the cost of building AI infrastructure.
The consumer discretionary and real estate sectors were also notable decliners.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_zh: Former Sacred Heart student Clavicular charged with raping 17-year-old
articles.content_orig:
Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
Clavicular, the controversial streamer who rose from the corners of the internet to the mainstream advocating for extreme tactics to achieve physical attractiveness, now finds his internet fame spilling into the courtroom.
Braden Peters, better known for his online moniker, has been charged in Massachusetts court with rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to an underage person, court records show.
Peters, 20, has become the visible face of the "looksmaxxing" movement. He’s gone to extremes such as hitting himself in the face with a hammer so his bones supposedly grow back sharper and taking small amounts of methamphetamine in an attempt to suppress his appetite. Offshoots of the trend, which are associated with the "manosphere," have ventured into sexist, misogynistic and racist philosophies, while Peters himself has drawn criticism for using racial slurs during his streams.
The viral nature of his controversial soundbites and short-form content helped usher what was once a niche subculture on obscure Reddit forums into the mainstream on TikTok, Instagram and Kik, where he’s collectively amassed more than 2.7 million followers. Now, the turn in his trajectory offers a window into the pitfalls of a movement drawing young men online in droves.
What is 'looksmaxxing,' the 'manosphere?'
"Looksmaxxing" is the process of maximizing one’s physical appearance through hygiene, fitness and style.
The term has gone mainstream and can have positive implications, such as getting healthy or working out more in the hopes of finding more confidence in the dating world.
However, the looksmaxxing movement has roots in online incel culture, which villainizes women, and has become a new subset of the "manosphere," a digital collection of websites, videos and social media that promote male supremacy and advocate for traditional gender roles.
How young men get sucked into 'looksmaxxing'
The combination of technology and the natural insecurities that arise during teenage years creates a "perfect storm" for innocuous sports and health spaces to tune young men into radical content, Gary Barker, the president of Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, an organization that advocates for healthy manhood, previously told USA TODAY.
"They’re going there with kind of innocent intentions, but without somebody else supporting them, that innocent intention can become a follower who drops their critical thinking," Barker said.
Looksmaxxing creators have become a modern extension for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Among these creators, such as Kareem Shami, an early adopter who encourages "mewing," and Alex Costa, who focuses on "softmaxxing" with style and haircare, Clavicular has become the most extreme, advocating for surgical upgrades. In June, he livestreamed his rhinoplasty on Kick, undergoing four procedures ahead of Paris Fashion Week in what he called "Ascension Week."
As his looksmaxxing tactics have been more extreme, so have his far-right, sexist and racist rhetoric.
His streams often feature degrading language regarding women, and he was seen partying in Miami with Andrew and Tristan Tate, manosphere creator Sneako and far-right nationalist Nick Fuentes in January, where the group was filmed singing along to Ye’s "Heil Hitler."
On Sept. 4, Romanian prosecutors indicted 39-year-old Andrew Tate for allegedly trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering, and his 38-year-old brother Tristan Tate for alleged complicity.
"The current version of the manosphere has become much more mainstream than it used to be," said University of Wisconsin-Madison public affairs professor Mariel Barnes, whose research focuses on backlash to gender equality and the manosphere. "You don't need to hide who you are anymore if you're a raging misogynist."
Extreme fringes of the manosphere have orchestrated or praised violent attacks against women, a trend Netflix’s 2025 crime drama "Adolescence" highlighted by following the story of a 13-year-old boy who was radicalized by misogynistic culture online.
Peters' September charges come after his teen protege Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza sued him in April for physical and sexual abuse after an incident at his Cape Cod, Massachusetts, home in May 2025. Mendoza alleged that the content creator had sex with her while she was intoxicated and without consent, and injected her with an "unapproved drug" during a livestream when she was 16.
Young men who tune into extreme content and are isolated from women and other men are more likely to take on radical views or engage in violence, according to Barnes.
"If you are constantly consuming this content and you are isolated and women are responsible for the bad things that are happening to you, it's very dehumanizing, right?" Barnes said. "You don't see women as humans anymore, or as peers or as friends, and that dehumanization gives you permission to treat them as less than human."
Taijuan Moorman and James Powel contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Stocks fall as yields shoot higher, Nasdaq retreats from record: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks fall as yields shoot higher, Nasdaq retreats from record: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026.
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
Declines in utilities and consumer discretionary stocks led the broader market's fall, shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.135%, its highest level since July 2007. It also saw its biggest one-day move since April 7, 2025. The 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since May 2024 at 4.947%.
2-year yield vs. 10-year yield, 1-day
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 66% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
During the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat.
U.S. equities finished in the red on Wednesday.
The S&P 500 shed 0.75% to 7,706.03, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 1.13% to 26,936.04. The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved down 352.10 points, or 0.68%, to 51,511.59.
Oil industry warns a diesel export ban will increase fuel prices
A driver returns a fuel nozzle after refueling a vehicle with diesel fuel at a Chevron gas staying in Tracy, California, US, on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026.
David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images
The oil industry has warned a diesel export ban will backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis as President Donald Trump weighs restrictions.
Trump appeared to back an export ban earlier this week, as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
All but two of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were falling in afternoon trading on Wednesday.
Energy led the way, rising about 1.1%. Industrials was the only other positive group on the day, up only marginally at about 0.2%.
Conversely, utilities was the biggest laggard, dropping 1.7%. Consumer discretionary and communication services weren't too far behind, notching a loss of 1.5% and 1.4%, respectively.
Market sees next Fed hike in October
Federal Reserve Board Governor Michael Barr speaks during a panel before the "Strengthening America's Economy Through Rural Investment: a Working Forum" hosted by the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, in Washington, D.C., U.S., April 14, 2026.
An October interest rate hike is very much on the table after a top Federal Reserve official Wednesday expressed support for one, and as fresh economic readings showed intensifying inflation pressures.
In remarks prepared for a housing conference in Chicago, Fed Governor Michael Barr said he thinks policymakers still have more work to do even after last week's quarter percentage point increase.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he said. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that." Read more.
Stocks making big moves: McDonald's, Cracker Barrel Old Country Store, Worthington Enterprises
Check out some of the companies making the biggest moves midday:
McDonald's — CEO Chris Kempczinski said at an investor day event he expects high inflation and flat traffic will continue to weigh on the restaurant industry. The burger chain reported U.S. same-store sales growth of just 0.8% in its most recent quarter as traffic to its domestic restaurants fell. McDonald's shares fell more than 5% to their lowest since 2022.
Cracker Barrel Old Country Store — The restaurant chain climbed 5% after reporting fiscal fourth-quarter adjusted earnings per share of 99 cents, up from 74 cents last year. Revenue of $849.3 million beat the consensus Wall Street estimate of $834.6 million, according to FactSet data, while restaurant level profit margins, cost of goods sold and adjusted EBITDA margins were all better than expected.
Worthington Enterprises — The industrial manufacturing company rose 4% on an encouraging outlook from leadership. CEO Joseph Hayek said the company is seeing opportunities across its business, "including rapidly growing demand for our engineered [American Society of Mechanical Engineers] tanks used in liquid cooling systems for data centers." First-quarter adjusted earnings and revenue surpassed the Street's estimates, according to LSEG.
McDonald's slides to its lowest level since 2022 as growth plan fails to impress
McDonald's Corp. signage on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Monday, Aug. 25, 2025.
Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images
McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.
Investors are not loving it: shares of McDonald's are down more than 5% in midday trading, on pace for their worst day since April 4, 2025 when they fell 5.7% and trading at their lowest levels since October 2022. The move extends a string of weakness: MCD is now on pace for its seventh straight weekly decline, which would mark its longest losing streak since August 2014.
Selig tells CNBC activity on "mentions" contracts are concerning
Michael Selig, President Donald Trump's nominee to serve as Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairman, testifies in a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on his nomination on Capitol Hill, Nov. 19, 2025.
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that activity on "mentions" contracts are "concerning."
The response comes after the CFTC informed some of its regulated entities on Tuesday that "mentions" contracts, where traders predict what one would say in a speech, televised event or earnings call, are susceptible to manipulation.
"I think a large number of these contracts have issues, and so we're going to take a hard approach in evaluating those," he said.

articles.title_orig: Meta's Muse rekindles fears over winners and losers as personal AI agent emerges
articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse rekindles fears over winners and losers as personal AI agent emerges
articles.content_orig:
The New York Times reporter Eli Tan using Meta Muse to buy movie tickets in San Francisco. Credit... Poppy Lynch for The New York Times
Reporting from San Francisco
Last week, I answered a call from an unknown number. “I reached Anthem Dental and am about to connect you,” a voice piped up.
The call was from an artificial intelligence “agent” created by Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram. Ten minutes earlier, the A.I. agent had called my dental insurer, given it my member ID, answered a security question and waited on hold before transferring me to the representative — just as I had asked it to.
I was surprised by how much easier the agent had made it to deal with insurance. It was one of many tasks that I accomplished with Muse , the A.I. agent app that Meta unveiled this month.
Muse is the first consumer A.I. agent from a major tech company that has become publicly available. The tech industry sees agents as the next frontier, far more capable than chatbots. Agents can roam the internet, sign in to websites, fill out spreadsheets and make phone calls on behalf of people — and that’s just the start.
To test Muse, I experimented with it nonstop for two weeks, giving over many aspects of my life to it. I had to trust Muse with my most personal data, which included connecting it to my bank accounts and email. Then I had it perform dozens of day-to-day tasks, including ordering my groceries, scheduling my meetings and setting my fantasy football lineups.
